title: KAFKA-21302:  Sort copartition groups and indexes for consistent Streams topology comparison
body:
Fixes KAFKA-21302

With `group.protocol=streams`, a member with identical copartition
constraints can be rejected because of differences in source topic
ordering. For example, constructing the same join with source topics
`["A", "B"]` and `["B", "A"]` can produce heartbeat copartition indexes
of `[0, 1, 2]` and `[1, 0, 2]`, respectively.

The coordinator compares these lists in an order-sensitive manner and
treats the second member’s request as a topology change. It returns
`INVALID_REQUEST`, causing the client to transition to FATAL and
preventing an otherwise valid instance from joining or replacing an
existing member

title: KAFKA-21389: Keep a ready streams member ready on ASSIGNMENT_DELAYED
body:
The group coordinator returns `ASSIGNMENT_DELAYED` in two situations:
during the initial rebalance delay of a new streams group, and when it
defers computing a new target assignment because the configured
assignment interval has not elapsed yet. In the second case the member
keeps its current assignment, but `StreamsMembershipManager` mapped the
status to `isGroupReady=false`. The membership manager then
re-reconciled the unchanged tasks as not ready, and `StreamThread`
skipped processing, committing and punctuating for all owned tasks until
a later heartbeat (up to one heartbeat interval) no longer carried the
status.

With this change, `ASSIGNMENT_DELAYED` on its own keeps the readiness of
the previous target assignment. Since the target assignment starts out
not ready and is reset when the member leaves or is fenced, a member
that has not been ready yet, including one waiting out the initial
rebalance delay, still does not enter `RUNNING` with an empty
assignment. A ready member keeps processing the tasks it owns. Missing
or incorrectly partitioned topics still mark the group as not ready,
also when reported together with `ASSIGNMENT_DELAYED`.

The new unit tests in `StreamsMembershipManagerTest` reproduce the issue
(a ready member owning a task receiving a second tasks-assigned event
with `isGroupReady=false`) and cover the combination with a
missing-topics status. The existing test for a ready/not-ready
transition without task changes now uses `MISSING_SOURCE_TOPICS`, since
it previously asserted the behaviour being fixed.

title: KAFKA-21374: Prevent cross-thread header leakage in global state stores
body:
Summary
This PR addresses KAFKA-21374, where global state store reads can receive incorrect record headers from the global processing thread.
While investigating the issue, I found that the global processor context retains headers from the record being processed. Since the same context is used by the global state store, other threads can receive unrelated headers during serialization and deserialization.
This can cause problems for applications that depend on record headers for deserialization.

Changes Made
* Updated GlobalProcessorContextImpl to allow the owning global thread to access its record headers, while returning empty contextual headers for reads from other threads.
* Updated GlobalStateUpdateTask to clear the record context after processing, including when an exception occurs.
* Added regression tests to cover header leakage during normal processing and concurrent global store reads.
* Added tests to verify thread ownership and record context cleanup.

Testing
I first reproduced the issue with a failing regression test and confirmed that the deserializer was receiving headers from an unrelated global record.
After applying the fix, I ran the relevant Kafka Streams tests.
* 323 selected tests passed.
* Sequential and concurrent regression tests passed.
* Both at-least-once and exactly-once test scenarios passed.
* Checkstyle passed.
* Spotless passed.
* SpotBugs passed.
* git diff --check passed.
The concurrent scenario was tested using TopologyTestDriver with controlled thread synchronization. I have not run a separate real-broker concurrency integration test.

title: KAFKA-21070: Fix task cleanup when state updater shutdown is interrupted
body:
When a thread is interrupted while waiting for task removal,
`shutdownStateUpdater()` exits before stopping the updater and closing
the remaining tasks. This can leave state stores and their resources
open.

  This PR addresses the interrupted-shutdown issue in KAFKA-21070. The
separate issue where the updater discarded tasks during shutdown was
already addressed by KAFKA-20721.

  This change continues cleanup after an interrupted removal wait. It
collects completed removal results and drains the tasks left in the
updater queues. Checking the futures is necessary because a task whose
removal completed after the interrupted wait is no longer in those
queues and can only be recovered through its future.

  `DefaultStateUpdater.shutdown()` also retries interrupted joins within
the original timeout. The updater must stop before the caller closes its
remaining tasks to avoid accessing them concurrently.

  An interruption alone does not cause shutdown to throw. Removal waits
remain interruptible. Once an interruption is observed, its status is
recorded and cleared so cleanup can continue. The calling thread's
interrupt status is restored in an outer finally block when shutdown
exits, including when cleanup throws. Leaving the status set during
cleanup would make the remaining steps fail early, such as closing the
thread producer or joining the task executor threads.

  ### Testing

  After merging upstream trunk:

  - `TaskManagerTest`: 182 tests passed    - `DefaultStateUpdaterTest`:
100 tests passed    - `StreamThreadTest`: 170 tests passed    -
Checkstyle and Spotless passed

  The regression tests cover interrupted cleanup, removal results
completed after the interrupted wait, and waiting for the updater to
stop. Reverting each corresponding fix causes its regression test to
fail.

  For successful late removal results, the test verifies handoff to the
task registry. For results containing an exception, it verifies dirty
close.

  Further tests check that the interrupt status is cleared while the
thread producer is closed and, with processing threads enabled, while
the task executors are shut down and the tasks to close are locked, and
that it is restored afterwards, including when the state updater
shutdown throws after the status was cleared.

title: KAFKA-21256: Fix reconciliation stalls in the Streams protocol client
body:
Fixes KAFKA-21256.

An `onTasksAssigned` failure can leave the consumer assignment different
from `currentAssignment`. The next reconciliation throws and leaves the
progress flag set, blocking further attempts even when a new target
arrives.

This change tracks partial progress through three fields:
- `reconcilingAssignment`: captures the target being processed,
independently of newer assignments received during reconciliation.
- `appliedActiveTasks`: tracks active tasks already applied to the
consumer, separately from the last successfully reconciled assignment.
- `revokedTasksSinceApply`: tracks successful revocations since the last
assignment application, preventing duplicate revocation during retries
and leave. Applying an assignment clears this history.

Reconciliation can now retry the same target or process a newer target
using the actual consumer-applied state.  synchronous failures clear the
progress flag, and successful reconciliation clears pending revocation
flags.

title: KAFKA-21228: Consider pending share updates in cold snapshot timer
body:
Ref : https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21228

Problem : 

ShareCoordinatorShard.snapshotColdPartitions() skips a run when every share partition's last snapshot was written by the cold snapshot job. The code infers this from `createTimestamp != writeTimestamp`, since only cold snapshots keep the original `createTimestamp` and move `writeTimestamp`. `ShareUpdate` records do not change either of these timestamps. so once every partition was cold snapshotted the timer kept skipping, even after new updates arrived.

Two fixes:

- `snapshotColdPartitions()`: skip the run only if every partition is cold snapshotted and has no pending share updates. Partitions are still picked by time since the last snapshot alone. Idle partitions with no updates must keep being re-snapshotted, because the prune floor is the lowest latest-snapshot offset across all share partitions.

- `handleShareSnapshot()`: reset `snapshotUpdateCount` on every `ShareSnapshot`. Previously it was reset only once the threshold was reached, so after a cold or initialize snapshot it still counted updates the snapshot already contained. This made the next threshold snapshot come early, and the count could not be used as a pending-updates signal.

`o.a.k.clients.CommonClientConfigs` is not part of the public interface
to Apache Kafka. It is neither in the javadoc nor is it marked
`@InterfaceAudience.Public`. However, a handful of the config keys for
producer, consumer, and streams were defined in this class, essentially
meaning that an application using the string constants was stepping
outside the Kafka public interface.

For example, `CommonClientConfigs.METADATA_RECOVERY_STRATEGY_CONFIG`
which is allowed as a producer config should really be
`ProducerConfig.METADATA_RECOVERY_STRATEGY_CONFIG`. The latter is in a
properly public class.

This PR adds all of the missing string constants to `ProducerConfig`,
`ConsumerConfig` and `StreamsConfig`.

It is debatable whether this is tidying up the code by implementing the
intent of KIPs, or whether it needs a KIP. For example, KIP-1242 added
`metadata.cluster.check.enable` as a config for producer, consumer and
admin. In explicably, the constant was added to `CommonClientConfigs`
(not public) and `AdminClientConfigs`, but not `ProducerConfig` nor
`ConsumerConfig`. This was a simple omission and was the intent of the
KIP (which I wrote).

title: KAFKA-20752: Respect logical schema when formatting dates
body:
`Values.convertToString(schema, value)` accepted a schema but never used it when
serializing `java.util.Date` values. `dateFormatFor(Date)` picked the format purely
from the millisecond value, so any `Timestamp` falling exactly on midnight UTC
(`getTime() % MILLIS_PER_DAY == 0`) was emitted as `yyyy-MM-dd`, silently dropping
the time component. Connectors producing timestamp headers (e.g. MongoDB source)
hit this via `SimpleHeaderConverter`; on the way back, `parseString` then yielded a
`Date` schema instead of `Timestamp`.
This change makes date formatting schema-aware:
- Adds `Values.dateFormatFor(Schema, Date)`, which selects the ISO-8601 pattern from
the logical type name (`Time`, `Date`, `Timestamp`) and falls back to the existing
millisecond heuristic when the schema is null or not a logical type.
- Threads the schema through `append`/`appendIterable` so dates nested in `Struct`
fields, array elements and map keys/values are formatted according to their
element schema. Key/value schemas are only consulted when the schema type is
actually `MAP`/`ARRAY`, since `ConnectSchema` throws otherwise.
- `Cast` SMT passes the field schema into `castToString`, so casting a midnight
`Timestamp` field to `STRING` keeps the time component. Schemaless casts are
unchanged.
The existing `dateFormatFor(Date)` and the `append`/`appendIterable` overloads are
retained and delegate with a null schema, so schemaless callers and subclasses see
no change.

Behaviour change: when a schema *is* present, it is now authoritative. A `Date`
schema value carrying non-zero millis within the day is emitted as `yyyy-MM-dd`,
and a `Time` schema value is emitted as `HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'` regardless of magnitude.
Previously both would have been guessed from the millisecond value.

title: KAFKA-19602: fix(streams): propagate state store names from KTable.transformValues to downstream KTable join
body:
## Change description

When `KTable.transformValues` is called with extra state stores (via the `stateStoreNames` parameter) and the result is not materialized, the resulting `KTableTransformValues` `ProcessorSupplier` did not expose those extra stores via `storeNames()`. As a result, a downstream `KTable` join operator had no way to learn about the extra stores and could not wire them through to the join processor, causing initialization to fail with `Processor ... has no access to StateStore ...`.

This change adds a new constructor to `KTableTransformValues` that accepts the `stateStoreNames` and merges them with the parent value getter's `storeNames()` so the full set of stores is reported. `KTableImpl` now passes the `stateStoreNames` it already received to this new constructor. Tests are added in `KTableTransformValuesTest` and `KTableKTableInnerJoinTest` to cover both the unit-level `storeNames()` behavior and the end-to-end join scenario from the issue.

### Testing strategy

Unit tests verify that the `view()` `storeNames()` method of `KTableTransformValues` returns the union of parent store names and the extra `stateStoreNames` when the result is not materialized. A new integration-style test in `KTableKTableInnerJoinTest` reproduces the exact scenario from KAFKA-19602: a `transformValues` on a `KTable` with an extra manually-added state store, followed by a self join, which previously failed during topology initialization.

title: KAFKA-19465: feat(connect): add value.type config to InsertHeader SMT
body:
This PR adds a new `value.type` configuration option to the `InsertHeader` SMT in `connect/transforms/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/connect/transforms/InsertHeader.java`. The option lets users specify the Connect `Schema` type for the literal value being inserted as a header, supporting `int8`, `int16`, `int32`, `int64`, `float32`, `float64`, `boolean`, `string`, and `bytes`. title: KAFKA-19902: fix(consumer): use latest leader epoch when committing offsets
body:
When the partition leader changes, the consumer's `FetchPosition.currentLeader` can become stale because it is inherited from the previous position and only refreshed when leader-change errors are observed. `SubscriptionState.allConsumed()` then committed `position.offsetEpoch` (the epoch of the last consumed batch) instead, which can reference log segments that have since been deleted by retention, causing `OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE` on the next session and an `auto.offset.reset` jump.

This change keeps `currentLeader` fresh by looking it up in metadata every time the fetch position is advanced in `FetchCollector`, and makes `SubscriptionState.allConsumed()` use the maximum of `offsetEpoch` and `currentLeader.epoch` (falling back to whichever is present) so that the committed offset epoch matches the most recent leader epoch known to the client.

title: KAFKA-19753: Fix duplicated topic metrics in FetchMetricsManager for topic names containing dots
body:
Since 4.1.0, `FetchMetricsManager` registers the KIP-1109 deprecated metrics (topic names with dots replaced by underscores) alongside the new verbatim-name metrics. The deprecated names were derived by string-wrapping the new-format metric name, which produced colliding and duplicated sensors when a consumer subscribes to topics whose names differ only by dots versus underscores (for example `my.topic` and `my_topic`), and left stale deprecated sensors registered when they should no longer be reported. Users scraping these metrics through Micrometer or Prometheus saw duplicated topic-tagged series.

This change:
- Derives the deprecated metric and sensor names through dedicated `deprecated*MetricName` helpers based on the mangled (dot-to-underscore) topic name, instead of wrapping the new-format name.
- Registers a deprecated sensor only when it does not collide with the sensor of a real topic whose name equals the mangled name, covering both registration orders (dotted topic seen first, underscore topic seen first).
- Adds `maybeRemoveDeprecated*` cleanup so deprecated sensors and metrics are unregistered once they should no longer be reported, including during assignment updates, with collision-aware removal so a still-assigned partition's metrics are never dropped.

The deprecated metrics themselves remain in place for topics with dots, as intended by KIP-1109, until their removal in Kafka 5.0.

Testing: five new unit tests in `FetchMetricsManagerTest` cover the dotted-versus-underscore topic interplay in both registration orders, topics without dots (no deprecated sensor registered), the partition-level lag/lead/preferred-read-replica metrics, and assignment updates. Verified with the scoped module run `./gradlew :clients:test --tests org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.FetchMetricsManagerTest`.

  state at build time so the shard-builder supplier closure can wire a
removal listener
  back into it.
- `BrokerServer` reads
  `groupCoordinatorConfig.streamsGroupTopologyDescriptionPlugin(...)`
and passes the
  resulting `Optional` through. When the config is unset the feature is
fully disabled.

### Heartbeat post-processing
- `StreamsGroupHeartbeatResult` now carries
`storedDescriptionTopologyEpoch` and
  `failedDescriptionTopologyEpoch` alongside `currentTopologyEpoch`, so
the service layer
  can decide whether to set `TopologyDescriptionRequired=true` without
re-reading the
  group.
- `maybeSetTopologyDescriptionRequired` applies the KIP-1331 gating:
plugin present,
  response has no error code, c
  initial delay; a successful push or a permanent plugin failure clears
the entry.
- The back-off is per broker (service-level), not per partition. To
avoid leaking entries
  for groups that vanish, `GroupMetadataManager` now exposes a
`Consumer<String>`
  streams-group removal listener (wired through
`GroupCoordinatorShard.Builder`). The
  listener fires from `removeGroup` whenever the removed group is a
streams group, and
  from the `STREAMS` branch of `onUnloaded`; the service registers it as
  `backoff::clear`.

### `StreamsGroupTopologyDescriptionUpdate` handler
- Synchronous pre-checks reject the request fast when the coordinator is
inactive
  (`COORDINATOR_NOT_AVAILABLE`), no plugin is configured
(`UNSUPPORTED_VERSION`), or
  the request is structurally malformed (`INVALID_REQUEST` for empty
`MemberId`,
  empty `GroupId`, or null `TopologyDescription`).
- The chain runs `validateStreamsGroupMember` *first* (so a fenced
caller gets
  `UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID` rather than an `INVALID_REQUEST` from a payload
conversion
  failure), then converts the wire payload to the broker-side POJO, then
calls the
  plugin.
- Plugin success writes a metadata record advancing
`StoredDescriptionTopologyEpoch`;
  a `StreamsTopologyDescriptionPermanentFailureException` (or a
synchronous throw)
  writes `FailedDescriptionTopologyEpoch`; any other exception is
treated as transient
  and writes no record.
- The client-visible error is always
`STREAMS_TOPOLOGY_DESCRIPTION_UPDATE_FAILED` with
  the plugin's message; the permanent-vs-transient split is
broker-internal.
- All back-off state mutations happen in a single `whenComplete`, driven
by a
  `BackoffAction` holder populated by each terminal branch. A
post-plugin write failure
  leaves the action at `ARM`, so the next heartbeat sees the drift and
re-solicits an
  idempotent re-push, matching the KIP-1331 invariant.

### `DeleteGroups` integration
- Before tombstoning, the service identifies retained group ids that are
streams groups
  with a non-default `StoredDescriptionTopologyEpoch`
(`streamsGroupsWithStoredTopologyDescription`)
  and calls `plugin.deleteTopology` for each in parallel.
- Per-group plugin failure surfaces as `GROUP_DELETION_FAILED` with the
cause string in
  `ErrorMessage`; the group is held back from tombstoning so the caller
can retry.
  Mixed batches are honoured: groups that succeed proceed to tombstone,
groups that fail
  return the per-group error.
- For DeleteGroups requests at version < 3 (pre-KIP-1331), the error is
downgraded to
  `UNKNOWN_SERVER_ERROR` with no message, matching the convention used
by KIP-1043 for
  new error codes that older request versions cannot interpret.

### Wire ↔ POJO converter
- `StreamsGroupTopologyDescriptionConverter` translates
  `StreamsGroupTopologyDescriptionUpdateRequestData.TopologyDescription`
into the
  broker-side `StreamsGroupTopologyDescription` POJO. Subtopology node
ordering and
  string-collection iteration order are preserved via `LinkedHashSet`,
so a downstream
  pretty-printer (e.g. the future `kafka-streams-groups.sh --topology`
command) can
  reproduce the source ordering.
- Wire-level node types (`SOURCE=1`, `PROCESSOR=2`, `SINK=3`) map to the
sealed `Node`
  hierarchy. `GlobalStore` shape is validated; a malformed payload
throws
  `InvalidRequestException`.

title: KAFKA-20666: Offset backing stores honor ByteBuffer remaining bytes
body:
JIRA: [KAFKA-20666](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20666)

### What

Kafka Connect offset storage uses `ByteBuffer` keys and values. The logical contents of a `ByteBuffer` are its remaining bytes, but three storage paths called `ByteBuffer.array()`:

- `KafkaOffsetBackingStore.set` (one site, both key and value)
- `FileOffsetBackingStore.save` (two sites, key and value)
- `OffsetStorageReaderImpl.offsets` (one site, value)

`ByteBuffer.array()` ignores `position()`, `limit()`, and `arrayOffset()`, and also throws `UnsupportedOperationException` for direct buffers. So a sliced or partially consumed buffer wrote or read different bytes than the caller supplied, and a direct buffer crashed the store.

Because Connect offset keys determine source partition identity, this could make a task fail to find its previous offsets on restart, duplicate work, skip records, or tombstone the wrong key.

Replaced the four `ByteBuffer.array()` call sites with `Utils.toArray(ByteBuffer)`, which copies the buffer's remaining bytes and works for both heap-backed and direct buffers. `Utils` was added to the import list of each touched file; no other code was reorganized.

### Tests

Added two regression tests that fail against the previous implementation and pass against the fix:

- `KafkaOffsetBackingStoreTest.testSetUsesByteBufferRemainingBytes` passes sliced `ByteBuffer.wrap("xkeyx", 1, 3)` and `ByteBuffer.wrap("xvaluex", 1, 5)` to `store.set` and verifies the underlying `KafkaBasedLog.send` receives only the `key` and `value` bytes, not the surrounding `x` padding.
- `FileOffsetBackingStoreTest.testSaveRestoreUsesByteBufferRemainingBytes` persists a sliced offset, starts a new `FileOffsetBackingStore` against the same file, and asserts the entry is recoverable under its logical `buffer("key")`.

### Validation

```
./gradlew :connect:runtime:test \
  --tests org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.KafkaOffsetBackingStoreTest.testSetUsesByteBufferRemainingBytes \
  --tests org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.KafkaOffsetBackingStoreTest.testGetSet \
  --tests org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.FileOffsetBackingStoreTest.testSaveRestoreUsesByteBufferRemainingBytes \
  --tests "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.FileOffsetBackingStoreTest.*"
```

Both new tests pass, and the existing `KafkaOffsetBackingStoreTest.testGetSet` and the full `FileOffsetBackingStoreTest` suite still pass on JDK 17.

### Scope

This PR targets the Connect offset storage path. The sibling tickets in the same `ByteBuffer.array()` cluster are addressed separately so each change stays small and reviewable:

- KAFKA-20657 (`JsonConverter`) — #22533
- KAFKA-20658 (`Cast` SMT) — #22534
- KAFKA-20656 (`Struct.getBytes` / `equals`) — coming as its own PR.

### Committer Checklist

- [x] Verified design and implementation
- [x] Verified test coverage and CI build status
- [x] Verified documentation (including upgrade notes) updates (no user-facing surface change beyond bug-fix behavior)

## Summary
Fixes [KAFKA-20657](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20657).
Kafka Connect `BYTES` values may be represented as either `byte[]` or `ByteBuffer`.

title: KAFKA-20644: Fail fast when admin.listeners overlaps listeners
body:
The Connect REST server supports a separate `admin.listeners` endpoint and handles three cases: 

1. unset (admin resources inherit the regular listeners), 
2. empty (admin resources disabled), 
3. distinct value (admin resources get their own connector). 

It did not handle the case where `admin.listeners` shares a host and port with listeners: `createConnectors()` builds a second Jetty connector on the same socket, which fails to bind at startup with an opaque "address already in use" error and no hint that admin.listeners is the cause. The code carried two TODOs acknowledging that it assumed the two were different.

Validate the configuration in `createConnectors()` before any connector is built, and throw a `ConfigException` when an admin.listeners entry shares a host and port with a listeners entry. The message directs the user to leave admin.listeners unset to serve the admin endpoints on the regular
listeners. Overlap detection treats wildcard hosts (0.0.0.0, ::) as binding all interfaces and ignores ephemeral port 0, which resolves to a distinct port per connector.

Also document the distinctness requirement on the `admin.listeners` config and remove the two stale TODOs.

Added unit tests covering exact overlap, wildcard overlap, distinct host:port, and ephemeral port 0. 
No KIP required: this only tightens validation of a configuration that already failed at startup.

title: MINOR: Reduce unnecessary offset reads during log recovery
body:
**LogLoader** computes recovery offsets after loading and validating the local log segments. In the branch where the log end offset may already be available, the previous code used Optional.orElse with _readNextOffset_ as the fallback.

Optional.orElse evaluates its fallback eagerly, so _readNextOffset_ could be called even when the existing log end offset was already present. Since _readNextOffset_ reads the next offset from the segment, this can add unnecessary work during log recovery.

This change keeps the behavior the same, but makes the fallback explicit so _readNextOffset_ is only called when the log end offset was not already computed.

title: KAFKA-20602: Bound DLQ topic creation, fix log level and restore interrupt in DeadLetterQueueReporter
body:
`DeadLetterQueueReporter.createAndSetup` verifies/creates the dead letter queue topic during sink task startup. The current implementation has three issues:

1. Indefinite hang on broker outage. Both `admin.listTopics().names().get()` and `admin.createTopics(...).all().get()` are unbounded blocking calls. When the broker is unreachable, each call blocks until the AdminClient's internal `default.api.timeout.ms` elapses (default 60s). Because tasks are started serially, a worker with N DLQ-enabled connectors can stall for up to N x 60s on a cold-broker scenario (DR failover, outage recovery), which surfaces to operators as "all connectors stuck Initializing".

2. Wrong log level. The expected "topic does not exist yet" case on first startup was logged at ERROR, even though the very next line creates the topic. This produces spurious ERROR alerts on every first start of a connector with DLQ enabled.

3. Interrupt status not restored. The `InterruptedException` handler threw a `ConnectException` without calling `Thread.currentThread().interrupt()`, clearing the interrupt signal for any upstream blocking call.

Changes:

- Bound both admin calls with `get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` so startup fails fast on an unreachable broker regardless of the AdminClient's configured api timeout, and add a `catch (TimeoutException)` that surfaces a clear `ConnectException`.
- Downgrade the "topic does not exist" message from ERROR to INFO and include the partition count and replication factor.
- Restore the thread interrupt flag before re-throwing on `InterruptedException`.

The 30s timeout is hardcoded rather than exposed as a new config to avoid a KIP; it covers the overwhelming majority of clusters and can be revisited if a user reports needing longer.

Testing strategy:

Added three unit tests to `ErrorReporterTest`. `createAndSetup` constructs its own `Admin` and `KafkaProducer` internally, so the tests use `mockStatic(Admin.class)` to inject a mock admin (and `mockConstruction` for
the producer), then stub the returned `KafkaFuture.get(timeout, unit)` to drive each path:

- `createAndSetupTimesOutWhenBrokerUnreachable` - stubs a `TimeoutException` and asserts a `ConnectException` is thrown and the admin client is closed. Done with a mocked timeout rather than a real unreachable broker so the test is deterministic and does not wait the full 30s.
- `createAndSetupRestoresInterruptOnInterruptedException` - stubs an `InterruptedException`, runs on a dedicated thread (so the restored interrupt flag does not leak into other tests), and asserts the flag is set after the `ConnectException` propagates.
- `firstTimeDlqTopicCreationLogsAtInfoNotError` - uses `LogCaptureAppender` to assert the first-time creation path logs at INFO and not ERROR.

No new integration or system tests: the change is a localized fix to an existing code path with no new public surface or cross-component behavior.

title: KAFKA-10317: Global thread should honor shutdown signal during bootstrapping
body:
## Summary
This PR introduces a shutdown-aware bootstrap loop in `GlobalStateManagerImpl` and a `consumer.wakeup()` call during `GlobalStreamThread.shutdown()` that together let `KafkaStreams#close()` interrupt global-store restoration in progress, instead of waiting for the entire changelog to be replayed.

Ticket: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-10317

## Implementation
The global thread passes its `inErrorState()` predicate to the state manager, which checks it before each batch in the bootstrap poll loop and exits cleanly when shutdown is requested. The `wakeup()` call additionally interrupts any in-flight `poll()` so shutdown takes effect right away, even if the loop is currently blocked on a fetch. A matching WakeupException catch in the main update loop ensures clean shutdowns aren't reported through the uncaught-exception handler.

## Tests
Added unit tests in `GlobalStateManagerImplTest` covering the supplier check and `WakeupException` handling in both `restoreState` and `reprocessState`, and end-to-end tests in `GlobalStreamThreadTest` for the close-during-bootstrap scenario.

title: KAFKA-19536: Respect grace period for out-of-order stream joins
body:
KStream-KStream left joins currently emit an out-of-order left record as `left+null` as soon as the join window end is behind stream time, even if the configured grace period has not elapsed. That can produce an unmatched result and a later matched result for the same left record.

This changes the immediate emission check to wait until `windowEnd + grace` is behind stream time. Records that are still within grace stay in the outer join store, so a matching right-side record can still produce the join result.

I added a regression test that advances stream time past the window end but still inside grace, verifies the left record is not emitted as unmatched, then sends a matching right record.

No documentation update is included because this fixes the implementation to match the existing `JoinWindows` grace-period behavior and does not add or change any public API, configuration, or protocol.

- `./gradlew :streams:test --tests org.apache.kafka.streams.kstream.internals.KStreamKStreamLeftJoinTest.testOutOfOrderRecordWithinGracePeriod --no-build-cache --rerun-tasks`

After removing `StreamsPartitionAssignor` from the single bulk `AT_STALE_THREAD_WRITE_OF_PRIMITIVE` block it appeared in (trunk line 600), SpotBugs reports two fields with warnings:

- `configure`, `subscriptionUserData`, and `onAssignment` are all `ConsumerPartitionAssignor` / `Configurable` interface methods. The Kafka consumer invokes them from inside `poll()` (e.g. `ConsumerCoordinator.java:311` calls `assignor.subscriptionUserData(...)`, line 370 calls `assignor.onAssignment(...)`).
- `maybeUpdateSubscriptionVersion` is `protected` and only called from `maybeScheduleFollowupRebalance` (line 1544), which is itself reached from `onAssignment`.
- The package-private `uniqueField()` getter is only invoked by `StreamsPartitionAssignorTest`.

title: KAFKA-14490: Throw UncheckedIOException from LazyIndex
body:
## Background
[KAFKA-14490](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-14490) proposes replacing checked `IOException` with `UncheckedIOException` in the log layer, following the pattern already adopted by the raft module. The ticket description specifically calls out `LazyIndex`'s private constructor as a candidate for simplification once `IOException` is unchecked.

This is the first PR in the KAFKA-14490 series. Plan posted on the ticket walks through the remaining 17 files in dependency order.

## Changes
- `LazyIndex.get` / `renameTo` / `deleteIfExists` / `close` no longer declare `throws IOException`. `IOException` is caught at the file-IO boundary inside `IndexFile`, `IndexValue` and the loader, and re-thrown as `UncheckedIOException`. This mirrors `FileRawSnapshotReader` / `FileRawSnapshotWriter` / `Snapshots` / `FileQuorumStateStore` / `KafkaRaftLog` in the raft module.
- The private constructor changes from `(IndexWrapper, long, int, IndexType)` to `(IndexWrapper, IndexLoader<T>)`. The new `IndexLoader<T>` is a small `@FunctionalInterface` that allows the lambda to declare `throws IOException`. `forOffset` and `forTime` now pass a lambda that captures `baseOffset` and `maxIndexSize` directly.
- The previous `loadIndex` private method and its `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` switch on `IndexType` are removed. The remaining `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` on `get` is for the `(IndexValue<T>) wrapper` cast, which is structurally required by the `<?>` wildcard on `instanceof IndexValue<?>` and cannot be eliminated without a larger refactor.

## Scope kept minimal
External callers' method signatures (e.g. `LogSegment.offsetIndex() throws IOException`) are left untouched. Their `throws IOException` clauses become redundant since `LazyIndex.get` no longer throws checked, but Java permits over-declared `throws` and pruning them belongs in the follow-up PRs that convert the surrounding files. This keeps the blast radius of the first PR limited to `LazyIndex.java`.

## Verification
- `:storage:compileJava` clean.
- `:storage:test --tests "*LogSegment*" --tests "*Index*"` all green.
- `:core:test --tests "*LogSegment*" --tests "*UnifiedLog*" --tests "*LazyIndex*"` all green (covers the Scala `LogTestUtils` and `RemoteLogManagerTest` callers).
- `:storage:spotlessCheck`, `:storage:checkstyleMain`, `:storage:checkstyleTest`, `:storage:spotbugsMain --rerun-tasks` all clean.

## Committer review notes
Happy to split out the constructor cleanup into its own PR if reviewers prefer the IOException conversion be reviewed in isolation first.

* `numIterations` (non atomic RMW + stale write)

body:
Update `NOTICE-binary` and add `verify_notice.py`

`verify_notice.py` checks that `NOTICE-binary`contains every `NOTICE` text embedded in the third-party jars shipped by `releaseTarGz`, ensuring all upstream attribution notices are included in the distribution as required by the Apache License 2.0.

It extracts all NOTICE-like files from third-party jars, deduplicates them by normalised content, then searches the third-party body of `NOTICE-binary` for each one using a whitespace-tolerant match. It reports two lists and exits non-zero if either is non-empty:

- Leftover – content in `NOTICE-binary` not claimed by any upstream NOTICE (potentially stale).

title: KAFKA-21380: Move limit-reached records to ARCHIVING on failed transition rollback
body:
### JIRA
https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21380

### Problem

When the DLQ flow is enabled for a share group (KIP-1191), records whose delivery count reaches the limit are moved to `ARCHIVING` on the normal release path so they are written to the DLQ topic (`InFlightState.tryUpdateState` with `dlqSupportEnabled=true`).

However, the rollback path in `InFlightState.completeStateTransition(false)` - taken when a two-phase state transition fails (e.g. the persister write fails) and the acquisition lock has expired - archives the records directly:

```java
state = previousState.deliveryCount() >= rollbackState.maxDeliveryCount ?
    RecordState.ARCHIVED : RecordState.AVAILABLE;
```

This bypasses the DLQ flow entirely: records that should have been dead-lettered are silently archived and never appear in the DLQ topic. Note that `completeStateTransition(boolean)` has no access to the `dlqSupportEnabled` flag, so the rollback path cannot currently reach `ARCHIVING`.

Two related inconsistencies:

1. `ARCHIVING` (normal path) vs `ARCHIVED` (rollback path) for the same limit-reached condition.
2. The normal path evaluates the limit with the delivery count including the current delivery (`deliveryCount` incremented before the check), while the rollback path uses `previousState.deliveryCount()` - the counts differ by one.

### Fix

- Thread the DLQ-support flag through `completeStateTransition`; on rollback with an expired lock and the delivery count at the limit, records move to `ARCHIVING` when DLQ is enabled (mirroring `tryUpdateState`), otherwise to `ARCHIVED`.
- Start the DLQ flow (`initiateDLQAndArchive`) for batches that move to `ARCHIVING` in both the local rollback (`rollbackOrProcessStateUpdates`) and the persister-failure path, outside the partition lock as in the successful path.
- Derive the DLQ cause from the delivery count when the batch has no recorded cause.

### Testing

- New `InFlightStateTest` (5 cases), which also fills the existing coverage gap for `completeStateTransition`:
  - normal release path at the limit -> `ARCHIVING` (baseline)
  - rollback with expired lock at the limit, DLQ enabled -> `ARCHIVING`
  - rollback with expired lock at the limit, DLQ disabled -> `ARCHIVED`
  - rollback with expired lock below the limit -> `AVAILABLE`
  - rollback without an expired lock restores the previous state and member
  - The DLQ-enabled rollback case fails on trunk and passes with this change.
- Regression: `SharePartitionTest` (289), `SharePartitionManagerTest` (60), `ShareGroupDLQStateManagerTest` (71), `ShareGroupDLQRecordFetcherTest` (29) - all pass with the change.
- `checkstyle` passes for the changed modules.

title: KAFKA-20901: Enforce cordoned log directories configured with relative paths
body:
Kafka allows `log.dirs `to be configured with relative paths, but `cordoned.log.dirs` was validated and applied using the original configuration strings, whereas `LogManager` converts log directories to absolute paths and uses those paths for directory ID lookups.

As a result, configuring `cordoned.log.dirs` with the absolute path reported by `DescribeLogDirs` was rejected when `log.dirs` contained the equivalent relative path. Using the relative path passed validation, but it did not match the absolute path used internally, so the directory was not reported as cordoned to the controller.


This change consistently uses absolute paths when validating and applying `cordoned.log.dirs`, including during dynamic reconfiguration and broker heartbeat propagation.

title: KAFKA-21043: Do not share LoginManager across class loaders
body:
### Summary

`LoginManager` is cached by the JAAS configuration, the login class, the login
callback class and the `sasl.*` configs, but not by the caller's class loader.
Two deployments in one JVM with the same configuration therefore share a `Login`.

For SASL/OAUTHBEARER that never recovers. The refresh thread of
`ExpiringCredentialRefreshingLogin` inherits the context class loader of
whichever deployment acquired first. When that deployment stops the reference
count does not reach zero, `login.close()` never runs, and every later refresh
fails with `IllegalStateException: Trying to access closed classloader`. Once
the token expires the broker rejects any client that has to re-authenticate.

Adding the context class loader to the key gives each deployment its own
`LoginManager`, so the count reaches zero when a deployment stops and the
refresh thread ends with it. Applications with a single class loader, brokers
included, are unaffected, since the key is then identical for every caller.

KAFKA-21043 has the full failure sequence and the history of the cache key.

### Testing

`LoginManagerTest.testLoginManagerWithDifferentContextClassLoaders` covers
distinct instances across class loaders, sharing within one, and disposal when
one deployment releases every reference while another keeps an identical JAAS
configuration. Reverting the key change makes it fail.

```
./gradlew :clients:test --tests '*LoginManagerTest'
./gradlew :clients:checkstyleMain :clients:checkstyleTest :clients:spotlessCheck
```

title: KAFKA-14102: Create the OAUTHBEARER SaslClient from the local factory
body:
### Summary

`Sasl.createSaslClient` resolves a `SaslClientFactory` through the JVM-wide
security provider registry, and `Security.addProvider` keeps only the first
provider registered under a given name. With Kafka loaded in more than one class
loader, the registered `OAuthBearerSaslClientProvider` belongs to whichever
class loader got there first and cannot cast a callback handler from any other,
so only the first application in the process can authenticate. Class loader
isolation does not help, because `java.security.Security` is JVM-wide.

`OAuthBearerSaslClientFactory` now returns null instead of throwing when the
callback handler is not usable, which is what `SaslClientFactory` specifies and
which lets `Sasl` try the remaining providers. `SaslClientAuthenticator` then
falls back to the factory of its own class loader when the registry yields no
client, for the mechanisms Kafka provides itself.

The registry is consulted first, so a provider configured through
`security.providers` keeps taking precedence, and the fallback only covers a
path that fails today with `SaslAuthenticationException`. SCRAM is unaffected:
its factory passes the callback handler through without a cast.

KAFKA-14102 has the original report and the earlier discussion.

### Testing

`OAuthBearerSaslClientTest.createSaslClientReturnsNullForUnusableCallbackHandler`
covers the factory contract, and reverting that change makes it fail.
`SaslAuthenticatorTest.testSaslClientFromLocalFactory` covers the fallback
through the authenticator, including that it returns null for a mechanism Kafka
does not provide, so other mechanisms are still left to the registry.

```
./gradlew :clients:test --tests '*OAuthBearerSaslClientTest' --tests '*SaslAuthenticatorTest'
./gradlew :clients:checkstyleMain :clients:checkstyleTest :clients:spotlessCheck
```

title: Publish Develocity Build Scans for the Docker images
body:
Publishes a Develocity Build Scan for each image the `docker_build_and_test` and `docker_official_image_build_and_test` workflows build. A new `Setup Docker` step runs the Develocity Docker build agent beside the build, using the `setup-docker` action from `gradle/develocity-actions`. The agent captures what reaches BuildKit, so the Dockerfiles and the build commands stay as they are.

The scans go to develocity.apache.org under the `kafka` project, with the `DEVELOCITY_ACCESS_KEY` secret the Gradle builds already use. title: KAFKA-21316: Reuse nodes in PartitionStates to avoid retaining removed entries
body:
PartitionStates keeps its order in a LinkedHashMap and moves a partition
to the end with remove + put. HashMap.removeNode does not clear the next
field of the removed entry, so when two partitions of the same bucket
are updated in turn, every removed entry points at the entry created
after it. Once one of them is promoted to the old generation, young GC
treats it as live and copies every removed entry that follows it, and
the chain keeps growing for as long as both partitions receive data.

We hit this on a follower broker (JDK 21, G1, 16 GiB heap). A mixed GC
ran out of free regions (`Survivor regions: 1->0(0)`) and promoted the
fetcher's entries. Young GC pauses then went from 11 ms to 34 ms on
average and stayed there until restart. A heap dump taken 14 hours later
held 2,048,712 removed `LinkedHashMap$Entry` objects alternating between
the two partitions of one bucket of one fetcher's map.

The only condition is two partitions that keep receiving data, fetched
by the same fetcher thread, whose keys fall into the same bucket of that
fetcher's map. The remove + put has been there since KIP-74. Because the
removed entries form a linked list, one GC worker copies them one by one.
Without a broker, updating two such partitions in turn one million times
leaves 2,000,002 entries reachable from the first removed entry.

This change keeps the order in a doubly linked list of nodes looked up
through a HashMap, and moves the existing node to the end instead of
creating a new one. The leader side does the same rotation for fetch
sessions with ImplicitLinkedHashCollection, which also reuses the
element. `LinkedHashMap.putLast` would do this in one call but needs
Java 21, and clients still targets Java 11.

Behavior is unchanged: order, `partitionStateMap()` as a live
unmodifiable view, and `size()`. `stateIterator()` no longer supports
`remove()`. No caller uses it, and with the old code it left `size()`
stale.

Testing:
- New tests in PartitionStatesTest: an update reuses the entry (fails
  on the old code), and the map view is ordered, live and unmodifiable.
- PartitionStatesTest, SubscriptionStateTest, AbstractFetcherThreadTest,
  ReplicaFetcherThreadTest and ReplicaAlterLogDirsThreadTest pass.
- A randomized comparison against the old class (200,000 mixed
  operations, 5 seeds) observed the same order, values and sizes.

New PartitionStatesBenchmark (JDK 21, `-prof gc`, ns/op and B/op):

```

updateAndMoveToEnd 22   11.6 ns, 40 B   8.6 ns, 0 B
updateAndMoveToEnd 125  11.7 ns, 40 B   5.5 ns, 0 B
updateAndMoveToEnd 1000 13.3 ns, 40 B   6.5 ns, 0 B
stateValue 22            2.1 ns         2.3 ns
stateValue 1000          1.7 ns         2.0 ns
forEach 22              17.9 ns        13.2 ns
forEach 1000            1606 ns        1447 ns
```

```

100         3,142 +- 490     2,650 +- 34
500         17,843 +- 541    12,900 +- 31
1000        38,029 +- 2,148  32,881 +- 276
```

title: KAFKA-14359: Do not send a partition's next batch before its first batch of the epoch is acknowledged
body:
JIRA: https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-14359

## Problem

An idempotent producer (the default) can send a partition's second batch while the partition's first batch of the
producer epoch (sequence 0) is still in flight. If the first batch then fails with a retriable error that leaves it
out of the log (`NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER`, `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS`, a request timeout, a lost connection), the broker
has no state for the producer and accepts the second batch as the first one (KAFKA-19880). Every retry of sequence 0
then gets `OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER`. `TransactionManager.canRetry` retries it, because it is not the next
sequence after the last acked one, until `delivery.timeout.ms` expires. The records of the first batch are lost, and
the producer stalls on them for up to `delivery.timeout.ms`.

The common trigger is producing right after `createTopics()`: the metadata already shows leaders, but the partitions
are still loading. With a new 64-partition topic, 3,000 records of 10 KB, gzip, and 1,024 keys, the stock 4.3.1
client stalled in 19 of 20 runs against a fresh 4.1.0 broker and in 6 of 6 runs against a fresh 4.3.1 broker.
The usual workaround is to call `Admin.listOffsets()` for every partition before the first send.

A TRACE log of one stalled partition (4.3.1 client):

```
06:29:27.530 WARN Sender - Got error produce response with correlation id 4 on topic-partition hang-jvmtr-1-8167-45, retrying (2147483646 attempts left). Error: NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER
06:29:27.544 TRACE TransactionManager - ProducerId: 15439; Set last ack'd sequence number for topic-partition hang-jvmtr-1-8167-45 to 1
06:29:27.778 WARN Sender - Got error produce response with correlation id 15 on topic-partition hang-jvmtr-1-8167-45, retrying (2147483645 attempts left). Error: OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER
06:29:27.783 TRACE TransactionManager - ProducerId: 15439; Set last ack'd sequence number for topic-partition hang-jvmtr-1-8167-45 to 2
06:29:27.961 WARN Sender - Got error produce response with correlation id 33 on topic-partition hang-jvmtr-1-8167-45, retrying (2147483644 attempts left). Error: OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER
```

Sequence 0 fails with `NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER`, sequence 1 is acknowledged 14 ms later, and every retry of
sequence 0 then fails with `OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER` until the delivery timeout.

## Change

While a partition's first batch of the current producer epoch is in flight and not acknowledged, the accumulator
assigns no sequence to a new batch of that partition:

- `TransactionManager.isAwaitingFirstAck(tp)`: the partition has in-flight batches, and `lastAckedSequence(tp)` is
  empty.
- `RecordAccumulator.drainBatchesForOneNode` skips such a partition's new batch with `continue`. It does not stop the
  drain: `shouldStopDrainBatchesForPartition` makes the loop `break`, and the drain stores that partition as the next
  start index, so every other partition on the node would also wait for the first ack.
- `RecordAccumulator.partitionReady` does not count such a partition as ready, as it does not count a muted one.
  Without this, the sender sees a ready node, drains nothing from it, and polls with a zero timeout until the ack
  arrives (a busy loop).

Retries already have a sequence, so they are not affected; the existing `firstInFlightSequence` check still orders
them. After the first ack, pipelining works as before, up to `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection`.

## Why it is safe

- It only holds back a batch that has no sequence yet. No sequence, epoch, or retry logic changes.
- The wait always ends: the in-flight first batch completes, fails, or expires. On expiry, the existing
  unresolved-sequence and epoch-bump logic runs as before.
- It applies once per partition per producer epoch. For the idempotent producer, that is once per partition for the
  producer's life (and after each epoch bump). With transactions v2 (KIP-890), the epoch bumps at every commit, so
  it applies to each transaction's second batch per partition. The cost is up to one round trip before that batch.
- Other partitions are not held back (the `continue`, and a test for it).

## Measurements (transactions v2)

Broker 4.3.1 (one node, `transaction.version` 2, local Docker), Apple M4 Pro. 1 KB values, keys spread over the
partitions. A transaction sends its records at once, then commits; latency is begin to commit. The idempotent runs
send 100,000 records, then time 2,000 single-record sends. Medians of 5 rounds; the rule on and off alternate within
each round. The JVM client is 4.3.1 with this change compiled into its `RecordAccumulator`, switched by a system
property for the measurement only.

| Workload | Partitions | Records/txn | records/s with | records/s without | p50 ms with | p50 ms without | p99 ms with | p99 ms without |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| transactional | 1 | 10 | 8,303 | 8,132 | 1.10 | 1.12 | 2.18 | 2.44 |
| transactional | 64 | 10 | 3,320 | 3,303 | 1.21 | 1.26 | 26.96 | 28.12 |
| transactional | 1 | 2,000 | 111,233 | 113,109 | 16.68 | 16.41 | 38.70 | 38.84 |
| transactional | 64 | 2,000 | 210,611 | 196,150 | 8.98 | 8.31 | 20.10 | 25.89 |
| idempotent | 1 | - | 97,705 | 99,145 | 6.56 | 6.50 | 16.48 | 12.71 |
| idempotent | 64 | - | 229,271 | 197,608 | 6.64 | 6.66 | 16.27 | 13.81 |

Small transactions have one batch per partition, so nothing waits. Large transactions wait about one round trip per
transaction; the medians differ by less than the run-to-run noise on this machine. The same rule in a WebAssembly
build of the client (where a busy loop is much more expensive) showed no difference above the noise either: for
2,000-record transactions, 0.88-1.15 times the throughput without the change, over 15 rounds.

## Relation to other issues and PRs

- **KAFKA-19880 / #22619** (broker): makes the broker reject a non-zero first sequence when it has no producer state.
  With it, the second batch in the scenario above fails instead of being appended, and the first batch's retry
  succeeds. This PR fixes the client side for brokers without #22619 (all released brokers today), and it avoids a
  wasted round of errors and retries with brokers that have it. The two changes are independent.
- **KAFKA-15591** (fixed for 4.5.0): the broker rejects a non-zero first sequence on an empty log. That covers new
  topics on new brokers, but not a partition with records and no producer state (for example after the producer
  state expired).
- **KAFKA-18905 / #23663** (open): adds a similar new-batch check (`wouldExceedBrokerDeduplicationWindow`) in the
  same loop, also as a `continue`. The two conditions are independent, and the patches touch different lines:
  #23663 applies cleanly on top of this PR, and this PR applies cleanly on top of #23663 (checked with
  `git apply --check` both ways). If both are merged, the two `TransactionManager` checks could become one method
  ("may this partition get a new sequence now?"). `testEpochBumpWhenOutOfOrderBatchesRetriedAndFirstBatchExpires`
  (the KAFKA-15591 test) now starts after one acknowledged batch; #23663 does not change that test.
- **KAFKA-9199**: the other approach, failing or epoch-bumping a batch whose `OUT_OF_ORDER_SEQUENCE_NUMBER` cannot
  resolve. This PR prevents that state instead; the two can coexist.

## Tests

New:

- `SenderTest.testNoNewBatchSentUntilFirstBatchIsAcknowledged` (`NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER`, `NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS`,
  `REQUEST_TIMED_OUT`): the second batch is not sent while sequence 0 is in flight or retried, and both are delivered
  in order.
- `SenderTest.testPartitionAwaitingFirstAckDoesNotBlockOtherPartitions`.
- `RecordAccumulatorTest.testPartitionAwaitingFirstAckDoesNotStarveOtherPartitions`: the drain skips only the waiting
  partition.
- `RecordAccumulatorTest.testPartitionAwaitingFirstAckIsNotReady`: a waiting partition does not make its leader
  ready.

All four new tests (eight cases with their parameters) fail without the `RecordAccumulator` change.

Changed: 11 existing `SenderTest` tests sent several batches before the first acknowledgement, which this change
prevents. Ten of them now start with `sendAndAcknowledgeFirstBatch(tp0)` (a new helper), and their expected sequences move
up by one until an epoch bump resets them. Their scenarios are unchanged otherwise:
`testIdempotenceWithMultipleInflights`, `testIdempotenceWithMultipleInflightsRetriedInOrder`,
`testIdempotenceWithMultipleInflightsWhereFirstFailsFatallyAndSequenceOfFutureBatchesIsAdjusted`,
`testCorrectHandlingOfOutOfOrderResponses`, `testCorrectHandlingOfOutOfOrderResponsesWhenSecondSucceeds`,
`testCorrectHandlingOfDuplicateSequenceError`, `testExpiryOfFirstBatchShouldNotCauseUnresolvedSequencesIfFutureBatchesSucceed`,
`testExpiryOfFirstBatchShouldCauseEpochBumpIfFutureBatchesFail`, `testEpochBumpWhenOutOfOrderBatchesRetriedAndFirstBatchExpires`,
`testUnresolvedSequencesAreNotFatal`. `testAwaitPendingRecordsBeforeCommittingTransaction` now acknowledges the first
produce request before it expects the second one.

Run locally on trunk 6556669 with JDK 25: `./gradlew :clients:test --tests 'org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.*'`
(620 tests, all pass), `:clients:checkstyleMain :clients:checkstyleTest`, and `:clients:spotbugsMain` (all pass).
Not run locally: the system tests.

Outside Kafka's tree, the change was also tested against real brokers (a 64- and 256-partition new-topic race: the
stock client stalled in every run, the patched one in none; and leader moves, lost responses, and a broker restart on
a 3-broker cluster: no loss, duplicate, or reorder).

title: KAFKA-21285: Fix dynamic thread counts are lost on restart
body:
Dynamic thread count updates must be within [current / 2, current * 2]. On restart, the thread pools are created from the static configs, and the dynamic configs are applied by the first metadata publish. That publish folds all changes into a single update, so a sequence of valid steps such as `num.io.threads` 16 -> 8 -> 6 arrives as 16 -> 6 and is rejected. The node keeps the static thread counts. 

KAFKA-17431 reads the dynamic broker configs from the latest snapshot on startup, but changes committed after that snapshot still go through the first publish.

My proposed fix skips the [current / 2, current * 2] bounds while the first publish applies the dynamic broker configs, on both brokers and controllers. The later updates are validated as before. Thread count configs in scope for the fix:
- num.io.threads
- num.network.threads
- num.replica.fetchers
- num.recovery.threads.per.data.dir
- background.threads
- log.cleaner.threads
- the remote log manager thread pools
- mirror.num.replica.fetchers

title: KAFKA-21286: Share consumer bounds fetch-buffer wait when no partitions are assigned
body:
### Jira
* [KAFKA-21286](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21286): Share consumer may delay fatal startup errors while waiting for the first heartbeat

### Problem
Following KAFKA-19804, the initial heartbeat interval defaults to `request.timeout.ms` (30s) while joining the group to avoid busy-spinning. In `ShareConsumerImpl.pollForFetches()`, the wait duration on `fetchBuffer.awaitNotEmpty(pollTimer)` was calculated solely as `Math.min(applicationEventHandler.maximumTimeToWait(), timer.remainingMs())`.

When a member is joining and has not yet received assignments (`subscriptions.numAssignedPartitions() == 0`), `maximumTimeToWait()` returns the 30-second request timeout. If a fatal error (such as `GROUP_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED`) arrives from the coordinator, the background event handler enqueues an `ErrorEvent`, but the application thread was blocked in `fetchBuffer.awaitNotEmpty` for the full 30 seconds before exiting `pollForFetches()` to process background errors.

### Solution
Align `ShareConsumerImpl` with `AsyncKafkaConsumer` by capping the fetch buffer wait timeout at `retryBackoffMs` when no partitions are assigned (`subscriptions.numAssignedPartitions() == 0`).

1. Added `numAssignedPartitions()` to `AbstractSubscriptionState` and implemented it in `ShareSubscriptionState`.
2. Loaded `retryBackoffMs` from configuration into `ShareConsumerImpl`.
3. In `ShareConsumerImpl.pollForFetches()`, capped `pollTimeout` at `retryBackoffMs` when `subscriptions.numAssignedPartitions() == 0`.
4. Added unit tests in `ShareSubscriptionStateTest` and `ShareConsumerImplTest` to verify that fetch buffer waits and fatal error reporting during startup are bounded by `retryBackoffMs`.

title: MINOR: Stop the heartbeat thread when it fails with a fenced instance id
body:
When a heartbeat gets `FENCED_INSTANCE_ID`, the heartbeat thread sets
its failure cause. Its loop then disables the thread and waits on the
coordinator monitor. The thread does not exit.

The next `AbstractCoordinator.pollHeartbeat` call sees the failure, sets
`heartbeatThread` to null, and throws the cause. It does not close the
thread. A later `close()` calls `closeHeartbeatThread()`, which finds a
null reference and returns. So the thread
`kafka-coordinator-heartbeat-thread | <group>` waits until the JVM exits.
An application that recreates consumers after this error collects one
such thread per consumer.

The other fatal heartbeat errors (authentication, group authorization,
interrupt, unexpected errors) leave the run loop, so those threads end.

This change makes `pollHeartbeat` close the failed thread before it
drops the reference. `pollHeartbeat` already holds the coordinator
monitor, and `HeartbeatThread.close()` sets the closed flag and notifies
that monitor. The thread wakes up, sees that it is closed, and returns.
`pollHeartbeat` does not join the thread, so it does not block.

Testing: `testHeartbeatRequestWithFencedInstanceIdException` now closes
the coordinator after the fenced error and waits up to 2 seconds for the
heartbeat thread to stop. Without the fix, this test fails because the
thread is still alive. With the fix, it passes. `AbstractCoordinatorTest`,
`EagerConsumerCoordinatorTest`, `CooperativeConsumerCoordinatorTest`, and
`KafkaConsumerTest` pass.

I ran the tests at trunk commit f568b7b. There, `AbstractCoordinator.java`
and `BaseHeartbeatThread.java` are the same as on current trunk.
`AbstractCoordinatorTest.java` differs only by the KAFKA-20858 rename in
its setup (`SubscriptionState` to `ConsumerSubscriptionState`).

Notes:
- JIRA ticket: KAFKA-21327
- Rationale: this is a prerequisite for KAFKA-21326 _(Enable Gradle configuration cache)_ ~which blocks upgrade to Gradle 10: KAFKA-20102 _Preparations for Gradle 10_~ _update_: see this [jira comment](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21326?focusedCommentId=18129875&page=com.atlassian.jira.plugin.system.issuetabpanels%3Acomment-tabpanel#comment-18129875)

_Drafted with Claude, then reviewed and edited._

:x: **Pitfall**: 
- `build.gradle` opens the repository with JGit at configuration time to compute the `commit id` and the `RAT excludes`
- With the configuration cache enabled, Git.open starts external processes (`git --version`, `git config --system ...`) that Gradle cannot track, so it reports configuration cache problems and fails the build by default.

- Use providers.exec to run `git rev-parse HEAD` and `git ls-files --others --directory` instead. Gradle tracks their output as configuration inputs, so a new commit or a new untracked file correctly invalidates the cache.

- `.git` is now checked with `exists()` instead of `isDirectory()`, so builds in a git worktree (where .git is a file) also get the real commit id and run RAT.

This also removes an implicit dependency: since KAFKA-21086 the `org.eclipse.jgit` import in `build.gradle` relied on JGit being on the build script classpath transitively via the Spotless plugin; related PR :arrow_down: 
- #23450

**Note: `:generator` submodule keeps its own JGit dependency (fetched from `gradle/dependencies.gradle`).**

title: KAFKA-21111 [3/N]: Promote the standby of an orphan on a member that cannot report its progress
body:
This is the third change of the series that makes the warm-up task
refiner (KAFKA-20665) compatible with clients that speak version 0 of
the streams group heartbeat (see KAFKA-21111), on top of #23784.

A copy of a task on a member that does not report its restore progress
can never be observed to be caught up, so it is neither promoted nor
protected, like any other copy that is not caught up. There is one
exception, for an orphan: a stateful task that nobody holds as an active
task, whose target owner can be warmed up but holds no state for it. If
the target assignment also names the holder of the unobservable copy as
a standby holder of the task, the holder runs the task as temporary
owner while the target owner warms up. A holder that heartbeats with
version 0, or whose version is not known yet, is such a member.

Here the alternative to promoting a copy of unknown lag is a restore
from scratch on the target owner next to a standby task that would have
to restore anyway, whereas elsewhere the alternative is keeping a
running owner. If the copy turns out to be stale, the temporary owner
restores it as an active task before it processes anything, which is the
restore the target assignment demands of it as a standby holder anyway.
If it is close, the task resumes processing at once. The hand-over then
demotes the temporary owner to its standby task in place.

The refiner is not the default yet, so this change is not live. The
tests cover the promotion for a holder of version 0 and for one of
unknown version, and the cases where it must not apply: a holder that
reports being behind, a standby that the target assignment does not keep
on its holder, and a target owner that cannot be warmed up.

title: KAFKA-21034: Wipe the global state directory when the store is corrupted
body:
GlobalStreamThread#initialize already wipes the global state directory when
stateConsumer.initialize() throws InvalidOffsetException, but a corrupted state store is not
handled the same way.

When the RocksDB invalid-state check fails under EOS, RocksDBStore#openDB wraps the resulting
ProcessorStateException in a TaskCorruptedException. TaskCorruptedException is a sibling of
ProcessorStateException rather than a subclass. It therefore falls through to the generic
catch (StreamsException) in GlobalStreamThread#initialize, which calls
closeStateConsumer(stateConsumer, false), and the corrupted directory is left on disk. Every
restart hits the same state, which becomes a crash loop under an automatic restart policy such
as a Kubernetes StatefulSet.

This extends the existing InvalidOffsetException handler to also catch TaskCorruptedException,
closing the state consumer with wipeStateStore=true so the next start rebuilds the global
store from the changelog. GlobalStateUpdateTask#close already logs "Deleting global task
directory after detecting corruption" on that path, so the deletion itself was already
implemented, but it was never reached for this exception.

This PR also fixes a double-cleanup bug affecting the existing InvalidOffsetException path.
When a global store was already registered, the inner catch closed the stores, but the outer
catch attempted to flush them again. This could throw IllegalStateException before
startupException was assigned, causing start() to return without throwing and leaving the
thread state at CREATED. Clearing the local stateConsumer reference after cleanup prevents the
outer catch from closing it again.

The existing shouldDieOnInvalidOffsetExceptionDuringStartup test is updated to trigger the
exception during initialization: previously, equal beginning and end offsets caused it to skip
restoration polling and exercise the running-thread path instead. It now verifies that start()
throws with the expected cause and the thread reaches DEAD. Two new tests cover
TaskCorruptedException during startup, and the same case with another global store already
registered.

**Does this need a KIP?**
I do not think so, but I would like this confirmed. The wipe on the InvalidOffsetException
path was introduced in KAFKA-10306 (2020) and the wipeStateStore flag in KAFKA-8897 (2021),
both without a KIP. This change routes TaskCorruptedException through the existing
state-cleanup path. The double-cleanup fix ensures that initialization failures are propagated
by start() on both exception paths. These are bug fixes and introduce no new configuration or
public API. If that reasoning is wrong, please let me know and I will open a KIP instead.

**Verification**
- ./gradlew streams:test --tests GlobalStreamThreadTest: 19 tests, 0 failures
- ./gradlew streams:checkstyleTest streams:spotlessCheck: passed
- Re-verified after merging trunk to resolve the conflict with #23407.
- Removing TaskCorruptedException from the extended catch makes both corruption tests fail:
  the exception propagates unwrapped, so getCause() returns null instead of the expected
  TaskCorruptedException.
- Removing the stateConsumer reset makes the already-registered-store test and the existing
  shouldDieOnInvalidOffsetExceptionDuringStartup fail, because start() returns without
  throwing.

title: KAFKA-21111 [2/N]: Grant tasks at once to members that cannot be warmed up
body:
This is the second change of the series that makes the warm-up task
refiner (KAFKA-20665) compatible with clients that speak version 0 of
the streams group heartbeat (see KAFKA-21111), on top of #23761.

A warm-up task can only complete a migration if the coordinator observes
the target owner restoring it, which a member that heartbeats with
version 0 never allows, as it does not report task offsets. When the
target assignment moves a stateful task to such a member, the refiner no
longer stages the migration. It lets the target assignment through for
that task, so the current owner revokes it and the target owner takes it
over, as it would without a refiner.

The check sits after the readiness check, so that a move between two
members of one process still happens inside the instance, and before the
analysis of the incumbent and of the copies, so that a caught-up copy on
another process is not promoted as a temporary owner. That detour would
only postpone the same cold grant and add a second hand-over. The
version of the current owner is irrelevant: a member that processes a
task is hot by definition, and keeps it while a target owner that can be
warmed up restores it. If the target owner already holds a standby task
of the task, the client recycles it into the active task, so the grant
is warm in the common case, even though the coordinator cannot see that.

The refiner is not the default yet, so this change is not live. The
tests cover the grant, the missing detour through a caught-up copy, and
a current owner of version 0 that keeps its task.

title: KAFKA-21111 [1/N]: Tell the refiner which members may be given a warm-up task
body:
This is the first change of a series that makes the warm-up task refiner
(KAFKA-20665) compatible with clients that speak version 0 of the
streams group heartbeat (4.2 and 4.3), and with a coordinator failover
during which the coordinator does not know the version of any member. A
warm-up task is only useful if the coordinator can observe how far its
holder has restored it, which a member reports through the task offsets
of a version 1 heartbeat. A version 0 member never does, so it could
never be promoted from warm-up to active.

This change only provides the information, and nothing uses it yet. The
coordinator records the version of every member's last heartbeat as
transient state of the streams group, with the same lifecycle as the
reported task offsets: written in the heartbeat path, dropped when the
member is removed, and not known again after a coordinator failover
until the member heartbeats. It is deliberately not persisted, so that
it can never outlive the client that sent it. The refiner is handed an
immutable view of it, and decides itself which versions it can warm up.
A member that is missing from the map, because the coordinator has not
heard from the member since it loaded the group, has an unknown version.
The refiner ignores the new input for now; the following changes of this
series use it.

See https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21111. The tests cover
the group state and the versions reaching the refiner through the
heartbeat path.

title: KAFKA-21364: Keep the offset reset of a revived task closed before initialization
body:
Under exactly-once, a corrupted task (for example after a commit times
out) is closed dirty, which drops the records it fetched but has not
processed yet. It is then revived with its input partitions marked to be
reset to the committed offsets. That reset only runs once the revived
task is initialized and completes restoration.

With the classic protocol, StreamThread enforces a rebalance right after
the corruption, and any assignment that arrives before the revived task
is initialized has the same effect: handleTasksPendingInitialization
closes the revived task and a new task is created for the same task id.
The new task starts with no pending reset, so it processes from the
current consumer position, and the next commit moves the input offset
past the dropped records. Those records never reach the state store or
the changelog.

This change keeps the input partitions that a task closed while pending
initialization still had to reset, and hands them to the new active task
created in the same assignment, limited to that task's input partitions
that are still assigned to the consumer. ReadOnlyTask throws on the new
Task#partitionsForOffsetReset, like the other mutating and non-read-only
methods.

CommitTimeoutOffsetResetIntegrationTest reproduces the loss by delaying

title: KAFKA-20999: [2/N] Add rack-aware standby task assignment to sticky assignor
body:
Second part of rack-aware standby placement for streams groups. It wires
RackAwareStandbyPicker (#23790) into StickyTaskAssignor. Without
rack.aware.assignment.tags, the assignment is unchanged.

Rack diversity ranks above stickiness, so standbys are now assigned in
four steps:
1. Get the best condition for rack awareness, and traverse all the
previous member, assignor it back to a previous member if it satisfy the
condition
2. Assignor it to the least-loaded process that satisfy the best
condtiion
3. Assignor it back to previous member if it has room
4. Assignor it to least-loaded process with no rack constrain

A process has room while one of its members is below the per-member
quota on active plus standby tasks; a least-loaded pick goes to that
member. After each placement, the assignor reports the change to the
picker with updated(), or updatedAll() when the quota drops, since a
lower quota can take the room of any process.

StreamsAssignorBenchmark gets a rackAwareTags parameter with five tag
layouts, two of them with one host per process, and standbyReplicas=2.

title: KAFKA-21230: Pause task executors on byte limit
body:
#23728 pauses processing and punctuation while the uncommitted state
store bytes of a StreamThread exceed `statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes`.
That pause is in `runOnceWithoutProcessingThreads`. When processing
threads are enabled, task executors process records and run punctuators
independently of the StreamThread loop, so the pause does not stop them.
If a commit is skipped during a rebalance, or fails, the executors
continue to write to the state stores. The uncommitted bytes then
increase without bound, and the native memory of the transaction buffers
increases with them.

`StreamThread#maybePauseProcessingForUncommittedBytes()` now also sets
the pause on the processing threads, through the new
`TaskManager#setProcessingThreadsPaused`. `runOnceWithProcessingThreads`
calls it after `maybeCommit`. The scheduling `TaskManager` gains
`setProcessingPaused` and `processingPaused`.

`DefaultTaskManager` keeps the flag in a volatile field for each
StreamThread. It does not use `TaskExecutionMetadata`, because all
StreamThreads share that object. While the flag is set, `canProgress`
returns false, so `assignNextTask` assigns no task and
`awaitProcessableTasks` blocks. When processing resumes,
`DefaultTaskManager` signals the executors. While paused,
`DefaultTaskExecutor` does not process or punctuate its current task.
The task makes no progress, so the executor releases it through the
existing path for such tasks.

`GlobalStreamThread` does not need this change. One thread writes,
checks and flushes synchronously, and no condition skips the flush.

Both tests in `UncommittedBytesLimitIntegrationTest` now also run with
processing threads enabled.

### What Changed

- Updates `KRaftMetadataRequest` benchmark to more accurately represent
a real scenario by making replica and leader placements random. Also
adds a JBOD case where brokers have >= 1 directory.
- Gets the leader id for a `MetadataResponsePartition` without
constructing a `Node` object.

online directories so that `BrokerRegistration.hasOnlineDir` no longer
requires a binary search. The previous code is a regression from
ZooKeeper Kafka and can impact performance in JBOD deployments.

### Benchmarking

```
./jmh-benchmarks/jmh.sh -p topicCount=500 -p partitionCount=50 -p
logDirsPerBroker=1,16 -f 10 -prof gc
KRaftMetadataRequestBenchmark.testMetadataRequestForAllTopics
```

```
  ┌──────────────────┬─────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐
  │ logDirsPerBroker │  trunk  │   this PR    │    change    │
  ├──────────────────┼─────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ 1                │ 2.20 ms │ 1.57–1.65 ms │ −25% to −29% │
  ├──────────────────┼─────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ 16               │ 3.52 ms │ 2.50 ms      │ −29%         │
  └──────────────────┴─────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
```

### Alternatives Considered

Storing the `MetadataPartitionResponse` contents directly in-memory via
a LRU cache. Any per-partition state that is being stored by this class
means broker memory usage will scale further with the number of
partitions.

Augmenting the `PartitionRegistration` to contain the fields in the
`MetadataResponse` being computed at request time. I beleive this
approach requires a new MV so that `PartitionRecord` and
`PartitionChangeRecord` can contain the relevant information on disk.
This would mirror ZK the closest in that the controller is responsible
for building the contents of the metadata response, and brokers forwards
it to clients who request metadata.

PR is as minimal as possible for now.
