title: KAFKA-16304: Report file read errors from SslTransportLayer.transferFrom as such
body:
Follow-up to #23445, under the same ticket (resolved, fix version
4.5.0).

Since #23445, a failed send of fetched records is passed to a handler
that re-reads the region on the scheduler, and the log directory is
offlined only if the re-read fails too. The re-read is needed because
over PLAINTEXT `sendfile` reads the file and writes the socket in one
call, so a disk error and a socket error are the same bare
`IOException`. `SslTransportLayer.transferFrom` does not have that
problem: it reads the file with `FileChannel.read`, then encrypts and
writes, so it knows which of the two failed. As discussed on #23445,
this passes that on instead of finding it out again:

* `SslTransportLayer.transferFrom` throws a new `FileReadException`, an
  `IOException` with the position of the read, when `FileChannel.read`
  or `FileChannel.size` fails. A `ClosedChannelException`, from a
  deletion or a shutdown, is rethrown as is
  (`FileReadException.ofReadFailure`).
* `TransferableChannel.distinguishesFileReadFailures()` says whether a
  transport does that: true for TLS, false, the default, for
  PLAINTEXT.
* `FileRecords.writeTo` passes to the handler a `FileReadException`
  always, a `ClosedChannelException` never, and any other
  `IOException` only if the transport cannot tell a failed read of the
  file from a failed write to the network channel. A failure of its own
  `channel.size()` call before the transfer becomes a
  `FileReadException` as well, unless it is a `ClosedChannelException`.
* `LocalLog` reports a `FileReadException` as a failure of the log
  directory right away, without re-reading the region. Other failures
  are re-read on the scheduler as before.
* `LogDirFailureChannel.maybeAddOfflineLogDir` logs the error only when
  it takes the log directory offline, so that the failures that follow
  in a failing directory do not flood the log.

Consequences worth stating:

* On TLS listeners a disconnect no longer re-reads the region that was
  being sent. In the test notes, consumers killed mid-fetch over TLS
  for 5 minutes made the scheduler re-read 151 MB without this change
  and nothing with it.
* On TLS listeners a read error now offlines the log directory even if
  the region could be read again by the time of a re-read, e.g. after a
  transient media error. Before, such an error was attributed to the
  socket. This is the criterion `LocalLog` applies to any other
  `IOException`.
* A failed `FileChannel.size()` call on the segment, over either
  transport, is now reported as a read failure without a re-read.
* For every caller of `maybeAddOfflineLogDir`, an error in a log
  directory that is already offline is no longer logged there.
* PLAINTEXT listeners still re-read: `sendfile` cannot tell the two
  apart.
* KRaft snapshots, sent through `UnalignedFileRecords`, are still not
  covered.

title: KAFKA-21230: Build RocksDB WriteBatch at commit
body:
`RocksDBTransactionBuffer` writes every staged write twice: to `pendingWrites` on the heap, which serves reads, and to a native RocksDB `WriteBatch`. The `WriteBatch` holds native memory for the whole transaction, and the buffer changes it while it holds the write lock.

The buffer now stages writes on the heap only. Writes to other column families and range deletes also stay on the heap until the commit. At commit, `prepareFlush()` builds the `WriteBatch` from the staged state outside the write lock, and `flushToBase()` writes it to RocksDB under the write lock. A JMH model of the two designs measured writes 2 to 7 times faster, and commits 8 to 12 times faster when the transaction overwrites keys. A commit with no overwrites and 1000-byte values is up to 28% slower.

Because no buffer writes to a backend at stage time now, the `stageToBackend` hook of `AbstractTransactionBuffer` has no function. This change removes it and all of its implementations.

The uncommitted-bytes estimate also counted a key once for each write in a transaction, so a key written many times could cause an early commit with little staged data. `AbstractTransactionBuffer.stage` now subtracts the size of the previous entry for the key before it adds the new entry. `RocksDBTransactionBuffer` uses this shared accounting for all of its staged data.

`statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes` now counts each staged write once. Before, it counted the heap copy and the `WriteBatch` copy. The commit still needs a native `WriteBatch`, but only for one store at a time, because stores commit one after the other. The extra memory at commit is therefore at most the uncommitted bytes of the largest store. A thread now commits early when its uncommitted bytes plus the uncommitted bytes of its largest store exceed its share of the limit. The global thread uses the same check. The limit is thus again a bound on the memory at commit.

The check uses the largest value of `StateStore.approximateNumUncommittedBytes()`, so it needs no change to a public interface. In-memory stores need no extra memory at commit, so applications with only in-memory stores commit early after less data than in 4.4. Applications with more than one transactional RocksDB store can buffer more data before an early commit. The 4.5.0 upgrade guide and the documentation of the config record this. The default stays at 64 MB.

title: KAFKA-21214: [8/8] Add the uniform2 consumer group assignor
body:
The uniform assignor balances the total number of partitions per member
but not the partitions of each topic: with homogeneous subscriptions, a
member can get all the partitions of a topic while the others get none
of them. The throughput is usually about the same across the partitions
of a topic but not across topics, so adding members does not spread the
load.

This patch adds uniform2, the next version of the uniform assignor, from
the steps of the previous patches. It lives next to the uniform assignor
while it is developed and is not registered as a built-in assignor. Its
assignments have these properties, in priority order:
- Every partition of every subscribed topic goes to exactly one of its
  subscribers.
- Every subscriber of a topic gets the same number of its partitions,
  the minimum quota, or one more, with an extra partition.
- No extra partition could move to another subscriber of its topic
  whose assignment is at least two partitions smaller.
- Partitions stay with their owners where the above allows. The
  placement moves the fewest partitions for the quotas, and an
  assignment that already has these properties is returned unchanged.
- The result is deterministic.

Changes:
- `Uniform2Assignor` and `AssignmentBuilder`, which reads the group,
  runs the `KeepStickyExtraPartitions`, `AssignRemainingExtraPartitions`
  and `BalanceExtraPartitions` steps on the quotas, places every topic
  and builds the result. Partitions of topics that a member does not
  subscribe to or which no longer exist are dropped. The class Javadoc
  of `Uniform2Assignor` describes the steps with a worked example.

title: MINOR: Speed up transaction index lookup with binary search
body: ### Motivation `TransactionIndex.collectAbortedTxns` sequentially reads and deserializes every index record from the beginning of the file. For a `READ_COMMITTED` fetch near the end of a segment with many aborted transactions, this can decode tens of thousands of records whose `lastOffset` is too old to overlap the fetch. ### Changes - Use binary search over the fixed-size records to find the first potentially overlapping record by `lastOffset` and the original termination point by `lastStableOffset`. - Retain a sequential path for fetches that overlap the first record, reusing the decoded first record to avoid regressions for reads at the beginning of the index. - Share the positional record decoder with the existing iterator. The on-disk format, public API, and per-record heap usage are unchanged. Both search keys are non-decreasing for valid Kafka-generated indexes: abort markers are appended in log-offset order, while LSO is the earliest remaining transaction's first offset, or the completed marker's offset plus one. A new out-of-order transaction-completion test covers this ordering precondition. The new tests also compare records, order, and `isComplete` against the sequential implementation over 1,000 generated fetch ranges, including the case where the LSO termination point precedes the first overlapping transaction. ### Tests - `./gradlew :storage:test --tests org.apache.kafka.storage.internals.log.TransactionIndexTest --tests org.apache.kafka.storage.internals.log.ProducerStateManagerTest.testLastStableOffsetDoesNotRegressWhenTransactionsCompleteOutOfOrder --tests 'org.apache.kafka.storage.internals.log.UnifiedLogTest.*TransactionIndex*' --tests 'org.apache.kafka.storage.internals.log.UnifiedLogTest.*ReadCommitted*' --tests 'org.apache.kafka.storage.internals.log.UnifiedLogTest.*Aborted*'` - `./gradlew spotlessApply checkstyleMain checkstyleTest spotlessCheck` ### Benchmark The included JMH benchmark was run unchanged before and after the optimization on Java 25, with 2 forks, 2 warmups, and 3 measurement iterations of 1 second each. All 18 parameter combinations improved, with non-overlapping 99.9% confidence intervals. These are hot-page-cache index-lookup microbenchmarks, not end-to-end fetch measurements.

title: KAFKA-20734: Avoid busy loop while transaction markers wait for an unavailable leader
body:
Follow-up to KAFKA-20734 (#22680).

Since #22680, markers for a partition without an available leader (for example an offline partition) stay in the unknown-broker queue of `TransactionMarkerChannelManager` until the partition has a leader again, instead of being dropped.

The sender thread retries these markers from `generateRequests()` by calling `addTxnMarkersToBrokerQueue()`, which always ends with `wakeup()`. While the leader is still unavailable, the marker is parked again, the wakeup makes the next `poll` return immediately, and the thread spins on `getPartitionLeaderEndpoint()` for as long as the partition stays offline.

The wakeup is not needed on this path: `generateRequests()` runs on the sender thread, and markers moved to a broker queue are drained later in the same call. This change:

- re-enqueues parked markers without waking up the network client;
- polls with a 100 ms bound while markers are parked, so they are retried after a backoff instead of in a tight loop or only when an unrelated event wakes up the thread (the same backoff `NodeToControllerRequestThread` uses for the same reason);
- keeps the wakeup for markers added from other threads and from completion handlers.

Since #22680 is not released yet, this should go together with it wherever KAFKA-20734 is backported.

### Tests
- `TransactionMarkerChannelManagerTest`: retrying a parked marker does not wake up the network client, and `doWork()` polls with the backoff while markers are parked and without a bound otherwise. Both tests fail without the fix.
- `TransactionsTest` (integration): commit while a partition hosted outside the transaction coordinator is offline, bring it back, and verify that a `read_committed` consumer sees the committed record. This covers the retry no longer relying on `wakeup()`.

title: KAFKA-20734: Return Node.noNode() for partitions with offline leaders in getPartitionLeaderEndpoint
body:
### Problem
Since the `KRaftMetadataCache` rewrite, `getPartitionLeaderEndpoint` returns `Optional.empty()` when a partition exists but its leader is not a registered broker, most importantly when the partition is offline (leader `-1`).

`TransactionMarkerChannelManager` interprets `Optional.empty()` as "partition deleted": it removes the partition from the transaction and completes the transaction without writing the marker. A commit/abort marker for an offline partition, including one re-enqueued after its leader failed, is therefore silently dropped. The partition is left with a hanging transaction and the commit marker is lost, so `read_committed` consumers stall on it.

### Root cause
A regression from the `KRaftMetadataCache` rewrite in [KAFKA-17573](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-17573). The previous Scala implementation returned `Node.noNode()` when the leader had no registered broker:

```scala
case Some(partition) => Option(image.cluster().broker(partition.leader)) match {
  case None => Some(Node.noNode)
  case Some(broker) => Some(broker.node(listenerName.value()).orElse(Node.noNode()))
}
```

The Java port mapped that case to `Optional.empty()`:

```java
.flatMap(partition -> Optional.ofNullable(image.cluster().broker(partition.leader))
    .map(broker -> broker.node(listenerName.value()).orElse(Node.noNode())));
```

### Fix
If the partition exists, `getPartitionLeaderEndpoint` returns the leader's endpoint for the listener, or `Node.noNode()` if there is none (leader offline, not registered, or without that listener). It returns `Optional.empty()` only if the topic or partition does not exist. The `MetadataCache` Javadoc now states this contract and why it matters: callers may treat `Optional.empty()` as a deleted partition.

### Testing
- `MetadataCacheTest#testGetPartitionLeaderEndpoint`: leader with endpoint, leader without the listener, offline partition, unregistered leader, unknown partition, unknown topic.
- `TransactionMarkerChannelManagerTest#shouldSaveForLaterWhenPartitionIsOffline`: with a real `KRaftMetadataCache`, the marker for an offline partition is kept in the unknown-broker queue, survives a retry, and the transaction is not completed.
- `TransactionsTest#testCommitMarkerIsWrittenAfterPartitionComesBackOnline` (integration): takes a partition hosted outside the transaction coordinator offline, commits, brings the partition back, and verifies a `read_committed` consumer sees the committed record.

All three fail without the fix and pass with it.

### Compatibility / risk
This restores the pre-KAFKA-17573 contract. All callers were reviewed:
- `TransactionMarkerChannelManager`: markers for offline partitions are parked and sent once a leader is available, instead of being dropped. `Node.noNode()` is never used as a destination.
- `NetworkPartitionMetadataClient`: already treats empty and `Node.noNode()` identically (`LEADER_NOT_AVAILABLE`).
- `ShareCoordinatorMetadataCacheHelperImpl` / share-group DLQ: already rejects both `null` and `Node.noNode()` leaders.

While a partition stays offline, the send thread re-checks its parked marker in a tight loop, because re-queuing the marker calls `wakeup()`. This is existing unknown-broker queue behavior: it applies today to a leader without the listener, and applied to offline partitions before KAFKA-17573.

JIRA: [KAFKA-20734](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20734)

Reported by Alyssa Huang. The issue was identified, and the fix sketched, by Artem Livshits.

**What**
KIP-714's client-metrics match config patterns are now validated with RE2/J syntax when a subscription's match value is new or has actually changed. A pre-existing subscription whose match pattern only compiles under java.util.regex is still compiled successfully, via a deprecated, temporary fallback that logs a warning.. **Why**
RE2/J guarantees linear-time matching, which matters here because match patterns are evaluated against client-supplied strings.

The switch needed care because RE2/J supports only a subset of regexes that java.util.regex supported and we wanted to ensure that existing match patterns compile even if they are not part of that subset.

title: KAFKA-21160 improve RequestHeader parsing on the broker
body:
`RequestHeader.parse()` derives the header version from the request API
version and parses the entire  header using that schema. For an API
version unknown to the broker, it falls back to the latest  supported
header version. If a future version adds a non-tagged field, parsing
fails with  `InvalidRequestException` and closes the connection, so a
newer client sending `ApiVersionsRequest`  never receives the v0
`UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` response needed to downgrade.

For unsupported API versions, `RequestHeader.parse()` now reads only
fields with a fixed layout across  header versions (API key, API
version, correlation ID, and client ID), leaving the rest unparsed.
Supported versions continue to be parsed as before.

title: KAFKA-20253: Fix high CPU loop after failed re-authentication
body:
**JIRA:**
[KAFKA-20253](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20253)

When re-authentication fails in the consumer (e.g., temporary OAuth
token server unavailability with SASL_OAUTHBEARER), the heartbeat timer
is left in an expired state. This causes `timeToNextHeartbeat()` to
return 0, leading the consumer poll loop to busy-wait with a 0ms timeout
- pinning a CPU core at 100% (ClassicKafkaConsumer) or 40-50%
(AsyncKafkaConsumer).

## Changes

### ClassicKafkaConsumer (AbstractCoordinator heartbeat thread)

The heartbeat thread's `catch (AuthenticationException)` and `catch
(GroupAuthorizationException)` blocks call `setFailureCause()` but never
call `heartbeat.failHeartbeat()`. This leaves the heartbeat timer
expired. After the user catches the exception and calls `poll()` again,
`timeToNextHeartbeat()` returns 0, causing the main thread to spin.

**Fix:** Call `heartbeat.failHeartbeat()` before `setFailureCause()` in
both exception handlers. This resets the heartbeat timer with
exponential backoff, preventing the 0-timeout spin.

### AsyncKafkaConsumer

Already fixed on trunk by #22836, so this PR no longer changes the async
heartbeat request managers.

## Testing

- Added `HeartbeatTest.testFailHeartbeatResetsTimerWithBackoff()` -
verifies that `failHeartbeat()` resets the timer to a positive backoff
value after expiry

## Reproducer

See https://github.com/mstruk/kafka-consumer-reproducer for a standalone
reproducer demonstrating the CPU spin with SASL_OAUTHBEARER.

title: KAFKA-20237: Re-enqueue InitProducerId request after authentication failure
body:
**JIRA:**
[KAFKA-20237](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20237)

When an idempotent (non-transactional) KafkaProducer encounters an SSL
handshake failure during the initial connection, the `InitProducerId`
request is dequeued from the pending requests queue but never sent. The
`AuthenticationException` is caught in `Sender.runOnce()`, which calls
`transactionManager.authenticationFailed()`. However, since the request
was already dequeued, `authenticationFailed()` iterates over an empty
queue and does nothing.

The `TransactionManager` remains stuck in `INITIALIZING` state:
- `bumpIdempotentEpochAndResetIdIfNeeded()` skips re-enqueueing because
`currentState == INITIALIZING`
- `nextRequest()` returns null because the queue is empty
- The producer becomes permanently unable to send messages, even after
the SSL configuration is corrected

## Changes

Added a recovery path in `bumpIdempotentEpochAndResetIdIfNeeded()` that
detects when the state is `INITIALIZING` but the pending queue is empty
and no request is in-flight. In this case, the `InitProducerId` request
is re-enqueued, allowing the producer to recover without requiring a
restart.

Also extracted the `InitProducerId` request creation into a helper
method (`enqueueInitProducerIdRequest()`) to avoid duplication.

## Testing

Added `testIdempotentProducerRecoversFromLostInitProducerIdRequest()`
that simulates:
1. Transitioning to INITIALIZING and enqueuing the request
2. Dequeuing the request (as
`Sender.maybeSendAndPollTransactionalRequest()` would)
3. Triggering `authenticationFailed()` (which does nothing since queue
is empty)
4. Verifying that the next call to
`bumpIdempotentEpochAndResetIdIfNeeded()` re-enqueues the request

## Impact

This enables self-recovery for idempotent producers in cloud-native
environments where certificate rotation or temporary auth server
unavailability can cause transient SSL failures. Previously, the only
workaround was to close and recreate the KafkaProducer.

title: KAFKA-20665: Report the end offset of a warm-up task with nothing to restore
body:
A standby task, and so a warm-up task, learned the end offset of a
changelog only from a restored batch. With nothing to restore -- an
empty changelog, or local state already at the end of an idle changelog
-- no batch ever arrives. The client then kept reporting an end offset
of Long.MAX_VALUE for the task, which the broker reads as an unknown
lag. The warm-up task therefore never counted as caught up, and its
migration stayed staged forever, holding a warm-up slot.

When the restore consumer of a standby task reports a lag of 0 for a
changelog without a restore end offset, the changelog reader now also
records the end offset, as the last offset like a restored batch does:
-1 for an empty changelog.

The reported end offset of such a changelog is now one past that last
offset, the next offset to fetch, as for the restore end offset of an
active task or of a source-topic changelog. A negative end offset would
otherwise be summed into Long.MAX_VALUE, and reach custom assignors
through the assignor API. A fully restored standby task now reports a
lag of 0 instead of -1 per changelog.

title: KAFKA-20665: Report active task restore progress the broker acts on
body:
A client reports the changelog offsets of an active task only while it
restores the task. The heartbeat carries offsets only when the
assignment changes, when streams.task.offset.interval.ms passes (default
60 s), or when a warm-up task is within acceptable.recovery.lag. So the
broker learned that an active task had finished restoring, or had come
within acceptable.recovery.lag, only with the next periodic report.
Until then the refiner took the owner to be restoring the task with an
old lag. It did not protect the owner as hot, and it granted a migration
off that owner cold instead of staging it behind a warm-up task.

The client now also sends offsets on the next heartbeat when an active
task it restores comes within acceptable.recovery.lag, and when an
active task that was in the last sent offsets has dropped out of them,
ie, finished restoring. The warm-up and active checks share one
predicate.

The refiner can still run on another member's heartbeat before the
member that finished restoring has sent its offsets. That window is now
at most one heartbeat interval, instead of the task offset interval.

title: KAFKA-20532: Defensive trimming of min.insync.replicas in controller and kafka-topics to tolerate whitespace-contaminated configs
body:
Summary :
Whitespace-contaminated min.insync.replicas values silently accepted at write time cause a controller failover loop and full cluster unavailability with no operator-visible warning, because the --describe observability path trims whitespace before displaying the value.

Impact
A topic config min.insync.replicas stored with leading or trailing whitespace (e.g. " 2") causes the KRaft controller to enter a continuous failover loop, making the cluster unavailable. The crash is triggered on every alterPartition event (e.g. any replica
restart), so recovery is not spontaneous. Critically, kafka-topics.sh --describe silently strips the whitespace before displaying the value, so the corrupted config is invisible to operators. There is no log warning, no alert, and no way to detect the problem via the standard Admin API observability path. An operator can stare at a failing cluster and see only
clean config values.

More Details in JIRA : https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20532

title: KAFKA-21276: Stop fetching standby changelogs while records beyond the limit offset are buffered
body:
A standby task whose store uses the input topic as its changelog may
only apply records up to the offset committed by the active task, but
`StoreChangelogReader` kept fetching beyond that offset. Those records
stayed in the restore buffer, which could grow until `OutOfMemoryError`
when the active task was far behind the end of the topic.

This PR pauses such a changelog partition while its buffer holds records
beyond the limit offset, and resumes it once the limit has moved past
them. This is how standby tasks worked before 2.5.0: `StreamThread`
paused the partition when `StandbyTask#update` returned records beyond
the limit, and this was lost in the refactoring of KAFKA-9113 (#7997).
The change adds no new config or public API.

The new test in `OptimizedKTableIntegrationTest` pauses the active task
and produces 1,000 more records: without the fix the standby polls all
of them beyond the committed offset; with the fix it polls once (at most
`max.poll.records`) and pauses the partition.

Related to KAFKA-19992 / KIP-1325.

title: KAFKA-21349: Wait for the high watermark before loading transaction metadata
body:
When a broker becomes the leader of a `__transaction_state` partition,
`TransactionStateManager` loads the log up to the log end offset. A
newly elected leader can have records above the high watermark that are
not committed yet and can still be truncated if leadership moves again,
even with clean elections. The coordinator then acts on state that is
later rolled back. For example, it can send COMMIT markers for a
PREPARE_COMMIT that the next leader doesn't have, and that leader later
times out and aborts the transaction, so the transaction is committed on
some partitions and aborted on others.

Loading with `FetchIsolation.HIGH_WATERMARK` is not enough, because a
new leader's high watermark can lag behind the true one, so the load
would miss committed records.

The coordinator doesn't write to the partition while it is loading
(requests get `COORDINATOR_LOAD_IN_PROGRESS`), so the log end offset at
the start of the load doesn't change. Once the high watermark reaches
it, every record the load reads is committed. This change:

- In `loadTransactionsForTxnTopicPartition`, if the high watermark is
below the log end offset, registers a `PartitionListener` and schedules
the load once the high watermark reaches the log end offset. The high
watermark is checked again after the listener is added, since an update
between reading it and adding the listener isn't delivered to the
listener.
- Abandons the load (removes the `loadingPartitions` entry) if the
partition is not online, becomes a follower, fails or is deleted before
the high watermark catches up. This runs on the scheduler, since
listeners are invoked with partition locks held.
- Skips partitions that are loading in
`removeExpiredTransactionalIds()`. On a leader epoch bump, the previous
epoch's cache entry stays until the new load replaces it, and tombstones
written for it would move the log end offset while the load waits.
- Logs the time spent waiting for the high watermark as part of the load
time.

In the normal case the wait is about one follower fetch round trip. If
an ISR follower is unavailable, the load waits until it is removed from
the ISR (`replica.lag.time.max.ms`). This does not cover unclean leader
election, where committed records can be lost.

Testing: added unit tests to `TransactionStateManagerTest` for waiting
for the high watermark, abandoning on each partition transition and when
the partition is not online, the high watermark advancing during
listener registration, a leader epoch bump while waiting, and expiration
of a partition that is being reloaded.

title: MINOR: Add streams group integration tests for the warm-up task lifecycle
body:
This extends the end-to-end coverage of warm-up tasks under the streams
group protocol beyond the scale-out case in #23608, with real Kafka
Streams clients against the real AssignmentRefinerImpl. The tests cover
the warm-up budget when two members join at once (only one migration is
warmed up while the other waits, and the waiting one is warmed up rather
than moved cold once the budget frees), and the scale-in mirror of
#23608, where a member leaving makes the target assignment no longer
want an in-flight warm-up task, which is then given up while its owner
keeps running the task. Warm-up revocation was so far only verified at
the coordinator level. They also cover the client reporting a warm-up
task's offsets on the next heartbeat once it is caught up, even with a
task offset interval far longer than the test, promotion being gated on
acceptable.recovery.lag (withheld at a known lag above the threshold,
promoted once the threshold is raised while the lag is held constant),
and tasks moving cold with no warm-up task when num.warmup.replicas is
0.

Where a test has to hold a warm-up task behind, the instance's restore
consumer, which unlike the main consumer is still taken from the client
supplier under the streams group protocol, lets a small budget of
records through and then withholds the rest. A budget is needed rather
than a gate that is closed from the start, since a warm-up task that has
restored nothing reports no offset, and there would be no lag to gate
on. EmbeddedKafkaCluster gains setters for the warm-up related group
configs, and setGroupHeartbeatTimeout is renamed to
setGroupHeartbeatInterval, since it sets streams.heartbeat.interval.ms
and the old name suggested a timeout.

The tests surfaced that a client reports an active task's restore having
finished only with its next offset report, which can be up to
streams.task.offset.interval.ms later, and that until then the refiner
takes the owner to still be restoring and moves the task without warming
it up. The tests therefore run with the shortest task offset interval
and wait for the broker to see all active tasks running before staging a
migration.

Tests for coordinator failover, the active owner leaving mid-warm-up,
and members with several stream threads follow in a separate PR stacked
on this one.

The test class passed repeated local runs (20 consecutive runs before
the split, with one failure traced to a race in the test itself and
fixed). Each key assertion was also checked against a mutation that
should break it: disabling the client's hot warm-up report trigger,
making isCaughtUp ignore the threshold, and making the refiner ignore
the warm-up budget each make the corresponding test fail.

title: KAFKA-21372: Build the PartitionGroup#readyToProcess log message lazily
body:
### The issue
`PartitionGroup#readyToProcess` formats a not-ready message on every call and `StreamTask` runs it per record. `StreamTask` logs that message at most once every 120s and discards the rest. Tasks that read a busy topic together with a quiet one pay this cost on almost every record.

### Why it happened
KAFKA-19682 (#20693) replaced parameterized `logger.trace` calls with eager `String.format` calls collected in a `StringBuilder`. `StreamTask#isProcessable` also resolved the message before `maybeLogNotReady` checked the log interval.

### The fix
- `ReadyToProcessResult` holds a `Supplier<String>`. `maybeLogNotReady` calls it only when it logs.
- The suppliers capture only immutable locals, so they are safe with `SynchronizedPartitionGroup`.
- The message for the partition that blocks processing is unchanged. When no partition has data, the message now lists the partitions past their idle deadline. Before, it printed a "fetched lag" line for each of them.

### Tests
- New `PartitionGroupTest#shouldNotFormatNotReadyLogMessageUntilRequested`. It fails on trunk and passes with the fix.
- `PartitionGroupTest`, `StreamTaskTest` and `SynchronizedPartitionGroupTest` pass unchanged.
- Microbenchmark with two partitions, one of them idle: 1435 → 85 ns and 3288 → 264 B per call while waiting; 1904 → 214 ns and 1128 → 344 B once the idle deadline has passed.

title: MINOR: Use Locale.ROOT for the SCRAM iteration count and remove the unused credential string format
body:
`ScramMessages.ServerFirstMessage.toMessage()` builds the SCRAM
server-first-message with `String.format("r=%s,s=%s,i=%d", ...)`.
Without an explicit `Locale`, `%d` follows the JVM's default locale, and
on a broker whose default locale uses native digits (for example
`ar-EG`, `fa-IR`, `bn-BD`, `ne-NP`; JDK 9+ CLDR data) the iteration
count is emitted as `i=٤٠٩٦` instead of `i=4096`.

RFC 5802 requires ASCII digits, and `ServerFirstMessage` itself parses
the count with `i=(?<iterations>[0-9]+)`, so every SCRAM handshake
against such a broker fails with `SaslException: Invalid SCRAM server
first message format: r=...,i=٤٠٩٦` (non-Java clients reject it the same
way).

This passes `Locale.ROOT` to that `String.format` call, as already done
for `toLowerCase()` under KAFKA-20638 and for the
`tools`/`server-common` modules under KAFKA-20646 (which does not cover
`clients`), and adds a test that switches the default locale to `ar-EG`
(guarded with `@ResourceLock(Resources.LOCALE)`) and verifies the
message still uses ASCII digits. The other `String.format` calls in
`ScramMessages` only use `%s` and are not locale-sensitive.

Following review, it also removes
`ScramCredentialUtils.credentialToString()` / `credentialFromString()`:
the ZooKeeper-era credential string format had the same `%d` problem but
no callers left outside its own tests, so the methods, their constants
and the tests that only exercised them are gone.
`ScramCredentialUtils.createCache()` and its test are unchanged.

Reproduced against the released `kafka-clients` 4.4.0 jar on JDK 25:
```
java -Duser.language=ar -Duser.country=EG ...
server-first-message on the wire =
r=clientnonceservernonce,s=MDEy...,i=٤٠٩٦
client parse                     = FAILED: Invalid SCRAM server first
message format
```

title: KAFKA-21230: Pause processing on uncommitted bytes
body:
During a long rebalance, a `StreamThread` can use native memory without
limit and fail with an out-of-memory error. When the uncommitted state
store bytes exceed `statestore.uncommitted.max.bytes`,
`StreamThread#maybeCommit` forces a commit. But `TaskManager` skips
commits during a rebalance, and `runOnceWithoutProcessingThreads`
continues to process records. Thus the uncommitted bytes continue to
increase. RocksDB keeps these bytes in a `WriteBatch` in native memory,
outside the block cache and the write buffers.

At the start of each iteration of the processing loop, `StreamThread`
now calls `maybePauseProcessingForUncommittedBytes()`, which checks
`shouldCommitDueToUncommittedBytes()`. Because `maybeCommit` commits at
the end of each iteration, the bytes exceed the limit at this point only
when that commit was skipped or failed. So the check needs no extra
state. While processing is paused, the thread does not process records
or run punctuators, because both write to the state stores. It continues
to poll, so the rebalance can complete, and it continues to call
`maybeCommit`. Processing resumes when a commit succeeds, or when a
commit on partition revocation flushes the buffers. The thread logs the
pause and the resume at INFO level.

This change decreases throughput during a long rebalance, but it
prevents the out-of-memory error. `GlobalStreamThread` does not need
this change, because one thread writes to its stores, checks the bytes
and flushes them, and nothing skips that flush. A separate pull request
will apply the same pause to processing threads.

Two new `StreamThreadTest` tests cover the change.
`shouldNotProcessOrPunctuateWhileUncommittedBytesExceedLimit` shows that
the thread polls and tries to commit, but does not process or punctuate,
while the commit is skipped.
`shouldResumeProcessingOnceUncommittedBytesAreCommitted` shows that
processing stays paused for the iteration in which the rebalance
completes, and resumes only after the commit succeeds.

title: KAFKA-20820: make symlinked log.dirs possible when on JDK17
body:
The issue already came up earlier on the mailing list https://lists.apache.org/thread/ro8mbk70xstywz5yw7mlm4yoswcfqlp5

The bug can be reproduced by pointing log.dirs to a symlinked path, e.g.:

/kafka/1/dd -> /navencrypt/1/kafka/kafka/1/dd

The storage format step attempts to write the required meta.properties file to the configured log directory and fails with:

Error while writing meta.properties file /kafka/3/dd:
java.nio.file.FileAlreadyExistsException: /kafka/3/dd

The broker later exits with:

java.lang.RuntimeException: No readable meta.properties files found.

Based on my research the root cause is  a bug in JDK's Files.createDirectories which was addressed in https://bugs.openjdk.org/browse/JDK-8294193 and shipped in JDK 20.

To conclude, Kafka 4.x is committed to use JDK17 and there is no real restriction on why symlinked paths could not be used for log dirs. Also this bug prevents to use certain tools like NavEncrypt which could handle encryption at rest.

I would propose a simple fix to also make symlinked log.dirs possible when on JDK17.

title: KAFKA-20895: Grant pre-vote once the leader has resigned
body:
## Summary

`FollowerState.canGrantVote()` rejects a pre-vote whenever
`hasFetchedFromLeader` is true, ignoring that the leader may have
already announced it is resigning. On a clean shutdown the first
preferred successor then collects only its own vote plus the resigned
leader's, which is not a majority once the quorum is larger than three,
so it loses and a lower-ranked node wins instead. Every graceful
controller shutdown wastes an election round.

The fix lets a follower know its leader has stepped down, and treats
that as grounds to grant a pre-vote:

- `FollowerState` gains a `hasLeaderResigned` flag and a
`setHasLeaderResigned()` setter.
- `KafkaRaftClient.handleEndQuorumEpochRequest()` calls that setter next
to the existing `overrideFetchTimeout()`, inside the block already
guarded by "still a follower" and "the request came from our own
leader". The flag is only set on a genuine resignation from the leader
we are following.
- The grant condition becomes `isPreVote && (!hasFetchedFromLeader ||
hasLeaderResigned) && isLogUpToDate`. Standard votes are unchanged.

## Test plan

- `FollowerStateTest.testPreVoteAfterLeaderResigned`: after a successful
fetch, a pre-vote is granted only when the leader has resigned and the
requester's log is up to date. A standard vote is still rejected.
-
`KafkaRaftClientPreVoteTest.testFollowerGrantsPreVoteAfterLeaderResigns`:
the follower fetches from the leader and rejects a pre-vote from an
up-to-date peer. It then receives an `EndQuorumEpochRequest` from that
leader and grants the same pre-vote. The test runs once, on
`KIP_1186_PROTOCOL`.

The earlier `RaftEventSimulationTest` case was removed. This behavior is
covered by the unit tests above.

title: KAFKA-21306: Drop tasks already on the new process when a static streams member rejoins
body:
In a streams group, one process must never hold the same task twice, for
example as an active task on one member and as a standby task on
another. The reconciler checks this only when it grants a task to a
member. A task that the member already holds and still has in its target
assignment is kept without the check.

A static member that rejoins under a new member ID gets a copy of its
previous member, including the previous member's assigned tasks. If the
member rejoins from a different process, the copied tasks move to the
new process with it, and none of them is checked. When another member on
the new process already holds one of those tasks, that process now holds
the task twice. A Kafka Streams client gets here when an instance
restarts under a new process ID, for example because its topology has no
persistent stores: if one stream thread rejoins and is given the standby
of a task before the thread that ran the task as active rejoins, both
threads are told to run the task.

With this change, when a static member rejoins from a different process,
the new member keeps only the copied tasks that no member holds on the
new process, in any role. The dropped tasks stay in the target
assignment, so the reconciler grants them again later with its usual
checks. Until then, a dropped task has no owner on the new process
instead of two. When the process is unchanged, or no copied task is held
on the new process, the member keeps all its tasks as before.

`testStaticMemberRejoinFromNewProcessDropsTaskHeldThereAsStandby` drives
the restart above with the sticky assignor and one standby replica. The
second thread rejoins first and gets the standby. The first thread then
rejoins and gets no active task, and the new process holds the task only
as a standby.

title: KAFKA-21367: Prevent stale recovery checkpoints from overwriting truncation checkpoints

A periodic recovery checkpoint can sample recovery points before log truncation and write them after the truncation checkpoint. The existing file lock serializes writes but leaves sampling outside the critical section. The resulting stale checkpoint can cause startup recovery to skip an unflushed segment.

title: KAFKA-21273: Make each streams assignment refiner call cheaper
body:
`AssignmentRefinerImpl.refine()` runs on every streams group heartbeat. This PR makes a call cheaper without changing the intermediate assignment it derives. Each commit is one optimization and can be reviewed on its own:

1. Return the target assignment right after the case analysis when it stages no migration.
2. Walk every task fewer times: count process load in the index walk, find borrowed standby conflicts through the target standby holders, and build that lookup only when it is read.
3. Sort only the decisions, not every stateful target active task.
4. Skip counting active tasks when the refiner returns the target assignment itself.
5. Resolve the stateful subtopologies once per call instead of per (member, subtopology) entry.
6. Find the tasks not on their target owner first, and return before indexing when there are none. This assumes the target assignment names one member per active task, as the rest of the refiner already does.
7. Compare task IDs directly instead of building a comparator chain per comparison.
8. Index only the tasks not on their target owner; the process load still counts every task.
9. Build the target standby holders only for those tasks.
10. Patch members copy-on-write instead of copying every patched member in full.
11. Keep borrowed and parked migrations in hash sets instead of tree sets.
12. Count active tasks only for members whose tasks differ from the target assignment.
13. Build the state-on-disk lookup only when the case analysis asks for it.

Besides the unit tests, each step was checked against the previous refiner on 20,000 random groups, with identical results.

`AssignmentRefinerBenchmark.refinerImpl`, 1,000 members, 5,000 stateful tasks, one standby, MIXED lag, budget 2, µs per call:

| Migrating | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 0% | 4,151 | 151 |
| 1% | 4,345 | 767 |
| 50% | 6,032 | 2,567 |
| 100% | 6,923 | 3,367 |

title: KAFKA-18905: Avoid out of order sequence errors from multiple in-flight batches
body:
JIRA: KAFKA-18905

The producer now tracks, per partition, how many batches it has sent
after the oldest in-flight batch, including the ones that have already
been acknowledged.   It stops handing out new sequences for that
partition once that number reaches 4, so the oldest batch can never fall
out of the broker's window before it is resolved. Retries are not
affected by the new check.

On a healthy connection the broker answers requests in order, so this
condition is never hit and nothing changes. It only kicks in during a
leader failover, where new batches for the affected partition are held
back until the stuck batch is resolved, at most `request.timeout.ms`.
This trades a bounded delay on one partition for the batch no longer
failing spuriously.

title: KAFKA-20803: Index batched read state responses once
body:
Follow-up to #22835 for [KAFKA-20803](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20803).

When many partitions share a `READ_SHARE_GROUP_STATE` batch, `ReadStateHandler` scans the combined response for every handler. title: KAFKA-19023: Implement snapshottable timers in the coordinator runtime
body:
This PoC makes `CoordinatorTimerImpl` snapshottable, aligning timer
state restoration with the Coordinator’s snapshot and rollback
lifecycle.

The main changes are:

1. `CoordinatorTimerImpl` stores a `TimerState` for each timer in a
`TimelineHashMap`, using the same `SnapshotRegistry` as the Coordinator.
2. `TimerState` contains the information needed to recreate a
`TimerTask`: its deadline, operation, and retry configuration. Scheduled
`TimerTask` instances are managed separately.
3. When a record append succeeds, the existing
`updateLastWrittenOffset(offset)` flow creates a snapshot at that
offset, including the timer state. Scheduled tasks continue running
unchanged.
4. If the append fails, `revertLastWrittenOffset()` restores the timer
state to the rollback target snapshot.
5. After restoring the state, `timer.onRollback()` cancels all currently
tracked tasks and schedules new tasks based on the restored `TimerState
entries`. Each task uses the time remaining until its original deadline,
or a delay of zero if the deadline has already passed

title: KAFKA-21344: Handle partition rotation for share fetches
body:
A share fetch hands its record budget to partitions in the order they
are read, so the partition read first  takes the largest share. Two
things decided that order earlier and together they could starve a
partition, hence changed the behaviour.

Earlier:
- `SharePartitionManager` rotated the fetch list by `sessionEpoch %
size`. The client bumps the epoch on both
  ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge, so in a poll-and-commit loop fetch
epochs step by two and the rotation is
  constant. One unpaired request flips the parity, and with two
partitions the rotation then undoes the
  session reorder on every fetch, so the same partition is read first
until the other starves.
- `ShareSessionContext` moved served partitions to the end of the
session from inside the response iterator,
  in the iteration order of the response map. That map had passed
through `HashMap` copies, so when every
  partition returned records the session ended up in hash order and the
same partition led every fetch.

PR:

This change removes the epoch rotation from the fetch path and makes the
session reorder deterministic from  the fetch order. The fetch order is
preserved through `ShareFetchUtils`, `ShareFetch` and `KafkaApis` with
`LinkedHashMap`s. `ShareSessionContext` reorders the session in one pass
before pruning the response:  partitions without records keep their
position at the front, and partitions with records are appended in fetch
order rotated by one, so the partition read first is read last next
time. `PartitionRotateStrategy`  is reduced to that rotation and the
unused `sessionEpoch` parameter of `fetchMessages` is dropped.

`ShareConsumerFairnessTest` adds cases for the epoch parity change, for
the first position rotating when all partitions return records with
explicit and implicit acknowledgement, and for an idle partition being
read first once it has records.

`SharePartitionManagerTest` verifies the session order across subsequent
fetches.

title: Fix authentication bypass in PlainLoginModule JAAS implementation
body:
This PR fixes a critical authentication bypass in PlainLoginModule, where login(), commit(), and logout() previously returned true unconditionally and did not perform any JAAS-compliant validation. In such a configuration, any authentication attempt could be treated as successful, effectively bypassing authentication.
Changes
Store Subject and options in instance fields and introduce a loginSucceeded flag to track successful authentication.
Update initialize(...) to assign these fields while preserving the existing behavior of adding username and password from options into the subject’s credentials.
Change login() to:
Validate that username and password are present and non-empty in options.
Verify that the Subject contains these credentials in public/private credentials.
Throw LoginException on any validation failure, and only set loginSucceeded = true on success.
Change logout() to:
Return false if no successful login occurred.
On successful login, remove the configured credentials from the subject and reset loginSucceeded, returning true.
Change commit() to return loginSucceeded and throw LoginException as per JAAS semantics.
Change abort() to:
Return false if no successful login occurred.
Roll back by removing credentials from the subject and resetting loginSucceeded when aborting an in-progress login.
Add a helper method to safely remove credentials from the subject without concurrent modification.
Security impact
Ensures that authentication cannot silently succeed without valid, configured credentials.
Aligns the module with JAAS best practices by using LoginException for failures, tracking login state, and cleaning up credentials on logout/abort.
Addresses CWE-287 (Improper Authentication) and removes the identified AuthBypass condition.

title: KAFKA-12641: RemoteLogMetadataCache: bound leader-epoch state and cache highest copied offset
body:
JIRA: KAFKA-12641

## Summary
This PR bounds per-leader-epoch cache growth in `RemoteLogMetadataCache` and defines `highestOffsetForEpoch` as a monotonic “highest successfully copied offset” watermark that is retained across retention-driven deletes.

## Problem / Motivation
1) **Unbounded leader-epoch state growth**  
`RemoteLogMetadataCache` keeps a per-leader-epoch `RemoteLogLeaderEpochState`. When all remote segments for an epoch are deleted, the epoch entry can become empty but historically was not removed, causing the cache to grow without bound over time (KAFKA-12641).

2) **Progress signal semantics**  
The management subsystem consumes `highestOffsetForEpoch` as a progress signal. This value should be a monotonic watermark of what has been successfully copied, and it should not regress or disappear due to retention-driven deletes.

## Changes
### 1) Bound leader-epoch entry growth (KAFKA-12641)
Remove a leader-epoch entry once all segments for that epoch have been deleted (i.e. the per-epoch state becomes empty) to avoid unbounded growth.

### 2) Make `highestOffsetForEpoch` a pure lookup of a monotonic watermark
Maintain a per-epoch `leaderEpochToHighestOffset` watermark:
- Updated on `COPY_SEGMENT_FINISHED` and merged via `max` (monotonic).
- `highestOffsetForEpoch(int leaderEpoch)` becomes a pure lookup into this map (no fallback / hidden side-effects).

Rationale: we now delete empty `leaderEpochEntries`, so `highestOffsetForEpoch` must not depend on per-epoch state that can be removed due to retention; otherwise the progress watermark could disappear and trigger recopy loops.

NOTE: The watermark may be **higher than offsets currently present in remote storage** after retention-driven deletes.

### 3) Documentation clarifications
Update Javadocs (both cache and public API) to explicitly state:
- This value is a monotonic progress marker used by the management subsystem.
- It is retained after delete transitions and may exceed offsets currently present in remote storage.

## Testing
Executed locally:
- `./gradlew :storage:test --tests org.apache.kafka.server.log.remote.metadata.storage.RemoteLogMetadataCacheTest`
- `./gradlew :storage:test`

## Files touched
- `storage/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/server/log/remote/metadata/storage/RemoteLogMetadataCache.java`
- `storage/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/server/log/remote/metadata/storage/RemotePartitionMetadataStore.java`
- `storage/src/test/java/org/apache/kafka/server/log/remote/metadata/storage/RemoteLogMetadataCacheTest.java`

title: KAFKA-21312: Implement snapshottable tasks in the coordinator runtime
body:
When a write fails, the runtime reverts the coordinator state, but not
the tasks scheduled by the reverted write operations. When those tasks
complete, their results may no longer apply to the coordinator state.

Delay submitting the tasks scheduled by write operations until their
batch is written, and cancel them without submitting them if their batch
is reverted. Operations without records do not open a batch, so when no
batch is open, their tasks are submitted immediately rather than waiting
indefinitely for the next write. Cancelling a task is not reverted with
the operation which cancelled it. It is expected that callers
re-schedule tasks if they are still needed.

Do the same in MockCoordinatorExecutor and
GroupMetadataManagerTestContext, for use in future tests that roll back
writes which schedule tasks.

Time#waitForFuture compares absolute nanoTime values directly (`deadlineNs <= nowNs` and `deadlineNs - nowNs`). As noted in the JDK docs for System.nanoTime(), comparing absolute nanoTimes is unsafe due to potential overflow (wrap-around).

title: KAFKA-21234: FileRecords#readInto should honor slice boundaries (#23737)
body:
Cherry-pick of #23737 to the `4.2` branch.

When the metadata layer (e.g. `MetadataLoader`) reads a slice of records
from KRaft that is larger than `KafkaRaftClient#MAX_BATCH_SIZE_BYTES`,
`RecordsIterator` can return records past the end of the slice (the
HWM). `FileRecords#readInto` reads up to the end of the underlying file
instead of the end of the `FileRecords` slice, which can lead to a
metadata error where the node tries to snapshot with records past the
HWM.

This change bounds `FileRecords#readInto` to the end of the
`FileRecords` object, so reading a `[start position, HWM)` slice never
reads bytes past the HWM into memory. `RecordsIterator` also stops
growing its buffer once it has read the whole slice, since a trailing
partial batch can't be completed.

title: KAFKA-21234: FileRecords#readInto should honor slice boundaries (#23737)
body:
Cherry-pick of #23737 to the `3.9` branch.

When the metadata layer (e.g. `MetadataLoader`) reads a slice of records from KRaft that is larger than `KafkaRaftClient#MAX_BATCH_SIZE_BYTES`, `RecordsIterator` can return records past the end of the slice (the HWM). `FileRecords#readInto` reads up to the end of the underlying file instead of the end of the `FileRecords` slice, which can lead to a metadata error where the node tries to snapshot with records past the HWM.

This change bounds `FileRecords#readInto` to the end of the `FileRecords` object, so reading a `[start position, HWM)` slice never reads bytes past the HWM into memory. `RecordsIterator` also stops growing its buffer once it has read the whole slice, since a trailing partial batch can't be completed.

title: KAFKA-21227: Speed up ColdStartStickinessIntegrationTest
body:
The classic protocol case of ColdStartStickinessIntegrationTest takes
about
73 seconds locally, while the streams protocol case takes about 23
seconds.
After the first phase, the test closes both instances and waits for the
group to become empty before the cold restart. With the classic
protocol,
the stream threads stay in the group on close, so the group only becomes
empty when both members are removed on heartbeat expiration, about 44
seconds after the close (the default 45 second session timeout). The
streams protocol case is not affected, because dynamic members leave the
group on close by default.

This sets session.timeout.ms to 6 seconds and heartbeat.interval.ms to 1
second for the classic protocol case, so the members expire shortly
after the first phase closes. The instances still close without leaving
the group. Closing with LEAVE_GROUP does not work here, because the
first instance's LeaveGroup triggers a rebalance that can assign its
tasks to the second instance before it closes, which creates extra state
directories.

Local runs of the classic protocol case on the same machine:

| | Before (2 runs) | After (10 runs) |   |---|---|---|   | Test time
|72.8s, 72.9s | 33.8s to 34.0s |

All runs passed. In these runs, the first phase closed in under 1
second, and the members expired about 5 seconds after that.

title: KAFKA-21117: Handle group type changes during replay
body:
When log compaction races with coordinator loading, replay can encounter
records of a different group type after the previous group's deletion
tombstones were compacted away. The current code rejects some of these
transitions and overwrites others without clearing the previous group's
bookkeeping.

This change handles type changes consistently during Consumer, Streams,
Share, and Classic metadata replay. A record of a different group type
removes the existing group through `removeGroup`; a value then creates
the new group, while a tombstone leaves it absent. This also removes the
special cases for simple Classic groups and prevents deletion replay
from leaving an empty simple group behind.

Depends on #23530. This branch includes its current head,
`9e456de2610a1ad09a82942b56030f5efa555d50`, for topic-subscription and
Share state metadata cleanup. Rebase onto trunk and rerun validation
after #23530 merges.

Coverage:
- Eight parameterized test families cover all modern record types
against the other group types, including ordinary and simple Classic
groups, plus Classic metadata replay against modern groups.
- The 158 cases assert the resulting group type or absence, old
bookkeeping cleanup, and snapshot rollback. Simple groups are created
through actual offset commit replay.
- The two consumer downgrade compaction replay tests from #23220 remain
enabled.

title: [POC] KAFKA-20171: Kafka Streams use topic ids. (other version)
body:
## Summary

One possible way to support server-side regex in the StreamsGroup Protocol is for the broker to send topic IDs, and for Kafka Streams to resolve those topic IDs back to topic names on the client side before using them.

The ConsumerGroup Protocol already follows a similar model: the broker sends topic IDs, and the client only consumes topics whose names it can resolve locally. This POC explores the same general approach for the StreamsGroup Protocol.

This change introduces the end-to-end plumbing for that model. The broker continues to produce the authoritative task assignment, while the client materializes that assignment into fetchable `TaskId -> TopicPartition` mappings using local metadata.

## Scope
This is still a POC.

The current implementation does not yet include server-side regex source topic support itself. However, the remaining path appears straightforward: the broker would resolve regex source topics and send the corresponding topic IDs to the client, while the client would relax the regex-related constraints accordingly.

Also, broken method signatures in JavaDoc and some test code have not yet been cleaned up in this POC.

## Layering
This implementation can be divided into four layers.

### (1) Broker Assignment Layer
The broker produces the authoritative assignment and includes resolved topic IDs by subtopology in the response. The source of truth at this layer is the full task snapshot.

### (2) Membership / Client Control Plane Layer
StreamsMembershipManager manages the broker assignment in this layer. It operates on the full task snapshot and is responsible for owned-task reporting to the broker as well as callback sequencing.

### (3) Materialization / Fetch Layer
This layer resolves the topic IDs received from the broker into topic names using client metadata, and builds the actual fetchable TaskId -> TopicPartition plan. The source of truth in this layer is the materialized subset, and active tasks in subtopologies with unresolved source topics are excluded here.

### (4) Streams Runtime Layer
Callbacks and task control-plane behavior continue to use the full task snapshot. In contrast, the TopicPartitions used for actual runtime assignment and revocation are based on the materialized subset.

## Current Behavior
In this POC, if even one source topic ID in a given subtopology cannot be resolved to a topic name, the active tasks for that subtopology:

1. are not registered in SubscriptionState as TopicPartitions, and
2. are not included in the Streams runtime active assignment.
Once topic id -> topic name resolution becomes possible, they are included again in the materialization plan during the next maybeReconcile(), and are then reflected in fetch and runtime.

## Intent
The key idea of this POC is to keep the broker authoritative at the task-assignment level, while allowing the client to materialize only the subset that is currently resolvable from metadata.

In the previous version, the response included ResolvedTopicIds as a top-level field, but in this version, Resolved Topic Ids are included within the ActiveTaskIds structure.

title: KAFKA-20437: Fix ssl.enabled.protocols dynamic reconfiguration not being applied
body:
`ssl.enabled.protocols` is documented as a per-broker dynamically reconfigurable config, but it was classified in `SslConfigs.NON_RECONFIGURABLE_CONFIGS`. Because `SslFactory.createNewSslEngineFactory()` only   
  copies keys present in `RECONFIGURABLE_CONFIGS` into `nextConfigs`, the new value is silently dropped. `DefaultSslEngineFactory.shouldBeRebuilt()` then sees no diff and skips rebuilding the engine, leaving the  
  old protocol set active. As a result, operators who restrict `ssl.enabled.protocols` to TLSv1.3 via kafka-configs.sh see the change reflected in broker logs but TLSv1.2 connections continue to succeed.    
                                                                                                                                                                                                               
  This PR moves `ssl.enabled.protocols` from `NON_RECONFIGURABLE_CONFIGS` to `RECONFIGURABLE_CONFIGS`. With this change, `createNewSslEngineFactory()` copies the updated value into `nextConfigs`, `shouldBeRebuilt()`
  detects the diff, and a new `SslEngineFactory` is instantiated with the restricted protocol set. A regression test is added to `SslFactoryTest` that configures both TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3, reconfigures to TLSv1.3
   only, and asserts that a newly created `SSLEngine` no longer advertises TLSv1.2.

title: MINOR: Add streams group protocol integration test for warm-up tasks
body:
This ports the scale-out warm-up scenario from
HighAvailabilityTaskAssignorIntegrationTest, which exercises the classic
protocol's client-side HighAvailabilityTaskAssignor, to the streams
group protocol. Under the streams group protocol, warm-up derivation
happens broker-side via an AssignmentRefiner, which defaults to a no-op
implementation, so the test enables the real AssignmentRefinerImpl
explicitly to get coverage of the actual warm-up behavior against a live
cluster with real KafkaStreams clients, which did not exist before.

The test proves the same property as the original: when a stateful app
scales out, the new instance is first handed a warm-up task rather than
being promoted to active immediately, and is only promoted once its
local state has caught up, at which point the promotion happens with
zero real state restoration because the warm-up's state is reused
directly.

Two mechanisms from the original test don't carry over and needed
replacements. There is no client-side assignment-listener equivalent
under the streams group protocol, since that callback is wired into the
classic protocol's client-side assignor, so warm-up assignment and later
promotion are instead detected by polling
KafkaStreams.metadataForLocalThreads() for a task moving from the
standby set into the active set. On the target-assignment side, the
streams group protocol currently only ships the sticky assignor, which
balances active task load across processes rather than doing plain round
robin, but its load-balancing quota math still forces one of the two
tasks in this scenario onto the new, empty instance's target assignment,
which is exactly the mismatch the refiner needs in order to stage a
warm-up. So the test works with the sticky assignor as is, and does not
need to wait for a more round-robin-like assignor.

The rack-aware parameterization from the original test was dropped,
since the streams group protocol's sticky assignor has no rack-aware
placement logic today, so that axis would not exercise anything
meaningful. The in-memory versus persistent store parameterization was
kept, since it is a pure client-side choice orthogonal to the group
protocol.

### Test plan

- Ran both parameterized variants locally against a live 3-broker
embedded KRaft cluster; both pass.
- Confirmed via logs that the new instance is assigned a warm-up task
before promotion (`warm-up tasks {0_1}`, no active task), and that the
state-restore listener reports zero restored records at promotion time.
- `./gradlew spotlessApply checkstyleMain checkstyleTest` is clean.

title: KAFKA-21309: Handle Metadata responses without topic names
body:
[KAFKA-21309](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-21309)

A consumer subscribed with `SubscriptionPattern` requests metadata by
topic ID. When an assigned topic is deleted, or the client may not
describe it, the broker answers its ID with an error and no topic name,
as the schema allows. The client did not handle the null topic name row.

This fix

1) `MetadataResponse` skips error rows without a name, as opposed to
throwing `IllegalStateException`.
2) Now that a `null` name can reach the response handler, it skips the
row. On a retriable error (e.g. `UNKNOWN_TOPIC_ID`) it also requests a
metadata update, else (e.g. `TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED`) it leaves the
Fetch response to raise `TopicAuthorizationException`

partitions and resolves newly assigned topics.

title: KAFKA-9998: Bound the I/O thread join in KafkaProducer.close(timeout)
body:
`KafkaProducer.close(timeout)` can block forever. After the timed join, `close()` force closes the sender and then joins the I/O thread with no timeout. If a user callback is blocking that thread, for example while the forced close fails the pending records, `close()` waits for as long as the callback does, so the timeout is not honoured. `close(Duration.ZERO)` hangs the same way.

Separately, `Timer.remainingMs()` can return 0 and `Thread.join(0)` waits forever, so the first, timed join is unbounded too when the close timer has already run out.

This change:
- caps the wait for the I/O thread after a forced close at `max.block.ms`, and logs a warning if the thread is still alive afterwards
- never calls `Thread.join(0)`
- documents the bound in the `close(Duration)` Javadoc

The forced shutdown normally takes milliseconds, so normal behaviour is unchanged: `close()` still waits for it, and the failed records' callbacks still run before `close()` returns. Only a blocked I/O thread now leads to a bounded wait instead of a hang. The new logic sits in two small helpers so that `close()` keeps its current structure.

An alternative is to bound the wait by the time left on the close timer, as the JIRA suggests. That keeps `close()` within its timeout, but whenever the timeout expires, callbacks and interceptors of the failed records would run after `close()` returns, while it closes the interceptors and metrics. Happy to switch if reviewers prefer that, or a different cap.

Testing:
- `testCloseWithTimeoutReturnsWhileCallbackIsBlocked` and `testCloseWithZeroTimeoutReturnsWhileCallbackIsBlocked`: a send callback blocks during the forced close, and `close(100 ms)` / `close(0)` must return. Both fail on trunk (`close()` is still blocked after 10 s) and pass with this change.
- `testForcedCloseStillRunsCallbacksBeforeReturning`: guards the unchanged behaviour, and passes before and after.
- All tests in `org.apache.kafka.clients.producer` pass locally (615 passed, 3 skipped; macOS, JDK 26), as do Checkstyle and SpotBugs for `clients`.

This complements #23857 (KAFKA-21132), which bounds the transactional abort during close.

title: KAFKA-21253: Always clear record collector offsets in closeDirty
body:
`RecordCollectorImpl.closeDirty()` aborts the open transaction before
calling `close()`, which clears the collector's changelog offsets. If
the abort throws, `close()` is skipped and the offsets are kept. This
happens with an `IllegalStateException` after a timed-out
`commitTransaction()`. The revived task reuses the collector, so if it
is closed clean while its wiped store is still restoring, those stale
offsets are checkpointed. The next restore then skips the missing
records.

This change moves `close()` into a `finally` block so the offsets are
always cleared. It also logs the abort failure at ERROR before
rethrowing. The caller still swallows the exception, and before this
change it was only logged at DEBUG, without the exception.

`CommitTimeoutDirtyCloseIntegrationTest` uses the fault proxy to
reproduce this. A delayed EndTxn leaves a commit pending, so the abort
fails. A later `ILLEGAL_GENERATION` on `TxnOffsetCommit` migrates the
thread, and the restoring task is closed clean.

The associated integration test replicates the issue and without the fix
in this PR it fails.

title: MINOR: Skip further reads from log for share fetches if max records reached
body:
On the slow path, `DelayedShareFetch.combineLogReadResponse` reuses the
data read in `tryComplete` and issues a second `readFromLog` for
partitions that became acquirable only at completion. The second read
was issued even when the already fetched data covered `maxFetchRecords`,
in which case `SharePartition.acquire` receives a zero budget and
returns empty, so the read was wasted.

The remaining record budget is now computed from the already fetched
data and the second read is skipped when nothing remains. Skipped
partitions are absent from the response, as share sessions already do
for partitions without data, and their locks are released on the same
path as before.

title: KAFKA-21234: FileRecords#readInto should honor slice boundaries
body:
When the metadata layer (e.g. MetadataLoader) tries to read a slice of
records from KRaft which is greater than
KafkaRaftClient#MAX_BATCH_SIZE_BYTES, the RecordsIterator can return
records which are past the slice (HWM). As it iterates through this
slice of  records, FileRecords#readInto reads from disk the minimum of
the bytes  until end of the file and the remaining space in the
associated buffer.  In the case of the former, this can lead to a
metadata error where the  node tries to snapshot with records past the
HWM.

For the metadata error to occur, the following three pre-conditions must
be met:

1. One committed read handed to a listener is larger than 8 MiB.
2. The segment file has bytes after the HWM, meaning records this node
already appended but that aren't committed yet.
3. For the error to actually show up, the snapshot generator emits a
snapshot from the resulting image before the HWM catches up.

The underlying cause is the same as KAFKA-20841. Thanks to @asdf2014
for working on this issue as part of
https://github.com/apache/kafka/pull/22963.

Change `FileRecords#readInto` which reads from the underlying file to
the minimum of:

1. The remaining space in the associated buffer, which in the case of
RecordsIterator is the minimum of the FileRecords' record size and
the batch size defined by KRaft.
2. The end byte position of the FileRecords object, rather than the end
of the underlying file. This ensures when a caller constructs a
FileRecords slice of [start position, HWM), no bytes past the HWM are
read into memory.

Armando García Sancio <jsancio@apache.org>, Jun Rao <junrao@gmail.com>,
Zhiyan Tang <ztang@confluent.io>, Chia-Ping Tsai <chia7712@gmail.com>

title: MINOR: Track share fetch offset metadata per DelayedShareFetch instead of SharePartition
body:
DelayedShareFetch estimates the available bytes for minBytes by
comparing the end offset with the cached LogOffsetMetadata of the fetch
offset. The cache was kept on SharePartition, so it outlived the request
which populated it. A partition that is read but trimmed from the
response, or whose request fails, kept a valid cache entry although its
fetch offset did not advance, which requires resets and made the read
path depend on state left behind by earlier requests.

Keep the metadata inside DelayedShareFetch for the lifetime of the
request, as DelayedFetch does with FetchPartitionStatus. The retries of
tryComplete in purgatory still avoid reading from the log, and the cache
can no longer go stale across requests, so the remote fetch reset is not
needed.

Add ShareConsumerFairnessTest to verify that two partitions with a deep
backlog are both served under record_limit acquire mode.

There are also cases where if a record is released where it was earlier
fetch then request has to go through timeout to fetch data. Those
scenarios are also handled by this fix.

title: MINOR: Resilience improvements on leadership change
body:
`ShareConsumeRequestManager` has complicated behaviour when leadership
or cluster  topology change. Additional testing and analysis has
suggested improvements  where the share consumer could get stuck in some
situations.

The specific fixes are:
- Replace the cached leader from metadata when metadata holds a strictly
newer epoch, so a
  refresh is useful even when the cached node is still in the cluster.
- Forget cached leaders for a node when a request to it cannot be
delivered, so the next
  poll re-seeds them from metadata and follows a leader change the dead
node cannot report.
- Request a metadata refresh when a partition error names no new leader,
when the topic is
  unknown, or when metadata refuses a redirect the cache accepted,
instead of waiting for
  the periodic refresh. Remove the dead top-level UNKNOWN_TOPIC_ID
refresh.
- Fail acknowledgements queued for a node which no longer has a share
session, rather than
  leaving them pending forever after the node disappears from the
cluster.

title: KAFKA-21341: Report a TLS close_notify without a TCP FIN as a disconnect
body:
When a TLS `close_notify` arrives in the same read as application data,
`SslTransportLayer.read` returns the data and leaves the close for a
later read, but `updateBytesBuffered` clears `hasBytesBuffered`, so the
Selector never reads the channel again unless a TCP FIN arrives. A peer
may close only its TLS write side and keep the TCP connection open
(RFC 8446 section 6.1, e.g. a TLS-terminating proxy), and a request on
that connection then waits for `request.timeout.ms`.

The channel now stays in the buffered-read set after a `CLOSED` unwrap,
and the next read throws `EOFException` once the engine's inbound side
is done, so the disconnect is reported at once, as it already is when
`close_notify` arrives without data. A scattering read returns the
bytes it has already read instead of losing them to that exception.

Testing: new tests in `SslTransportLayerTest`, where a TLS peer sends a
partial or a full response plus `close_notify` in one write and keeps
the TCP connection open. The client must report the disconnect within
5 s (and deliver the full response), including when the channel is
muted after the response and later unmuted. The tests fail without the
fix.

title: KAFKA-21318, KAFKA-20292: Compute GroupSpecImpl's assigned partitions lazily
body:
Replace GroupSpecImpl's inverted target assignment with a BitSet of the
assigned partitions of each topic, computed from the members' current
assignments on the first call to isPartitionAssigned. Only the uniform
homogeneous assignor calls isPartitionAssigned, so other assignors no
longer compute it.

This makes build in TargetAssignmentBuilderBenchmark ~40% faster for
homogeneous groups, because isPartitionAssigned no longer looks up
partitions in the inverted target assignment's TimelineHashMaps, which
are slower than regular maps.

It also fixes a bug where the assignor saw the partitions of members
removed in the same request as still assigned. The bug is not reachable
today, since we do not compute a new target assignment when a member
leaves, only on the next heartbeat, and static member replacement keeps
the replaced member's partitions assigned.

Remove ModernGroup's inverted target assignment, since it is no longer
read. For share groups, it was never correct, because a partition can be
assigned to several members of a share group, while the inverted target
assignment holds a single member per partition.

Rename buildAssignment in TargetAssignmentBuilderBenchmark to
buildGroupSpecAndAssignment, which builds a new group spec on every
invocation, so that the cost of computing the assigned partitions is
included, and replace buildGroupSpecWithoutOffload and
buildGroupSpecWithOffload with an assignorOffload parameter.

title: KAFKA-20400: Enable VersionedKeyValueStoreWithHeaders in DSL
body:
Ref https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/KAFKA-20400

This PR extends the KIP-1285 headers-aware state store infrastructure to versioned key-value stores. Prior to this change, KIP-1285 was implemented for timestamped, windowed, and session stores, but versioned stores silently dropped record headers on both the write and read paths.

Reviewers: Alieh Saeedi <asaeedi@confluent.io>
---

Record headers carry metadata (tracing IDs, schema references, auth tokens) that downstream processors and interactive query clients may need. Versioned stores (RocksDBVersionedStore) were the only remaining store type that discarded headers. This PR closes that gap.

---
 API changes:

VersionedRecord<V> -- Added Headers headers field with new constructors and a headers() accessor. Existing constructors default to empty headers (backward compatible).

Stores.persistentVersionedKeyValueStoreWithHeaders(String, Duration) -- Factory method returning a dual-interface supplier.

Stores.versionedKeyValueStoreBuilderWithHeaders(VersionedBytesStoreSupplier, Serde, Serde) -- Builder factory method.

RocksDBVersionedStoreWithHeaders -- Extends RocksDBVersionedStore, encodes headers into value bytes using [headersSize(varint)][headersBytes][rawValue] format before delegating to the parent store. Decodes on read.

ChangeLoggingVersionedKeyValueBytesStore -- Added put(key, value, timestamp, headers) override to forward real headers to the changelog instead of empty headers.

KeyValueStoreWrapper -- get() now returns VersionedRecord.headers() instead of empty headers; put() forwards headers to VersionedKeyValueStoreWithHeaders when available.
